Text:
LLB 1ST YEAR NON-LEGAL ELECTIVE MODULES 
PRESCRIBED FOR ALL PROGRAMMES: 
LLB 4 (7162), LLB 5 (7172) AND BCOM LAW (7211) 

Herewith is a short information blurb available to assist you in 
selecting the required non-legal module. 

Note: Not all non-legal modules are included in this document. 

------------------------------ 

HISTORY153 (HIS153) 
History and arguments: Selected themes in African histories from 
the tenth to the nineteenth centuries 

This course covers two case studies. In the  first, we  consider the formation of 
southern  African  kingdoms  or  states  in  the  early  1800s,  the  movement  and 
destruction of societies and chiefdoms in the 1820s, and settlement and movements 
thereafter. There have been many views put forward by historians about the role of 
Shaka,  of  slave  traders,  of  settlers,  and  of  changes  to  land,  economies,  social 
formations,  and  the  environment  when  trying  to  explain  the  massive  shifts  of 
migration, state formation, and colonization, occurring on the south-east part of the 
continent in the ‘late-independent period’ of the early 19thcentury. 

In  this  course,  we  explore  two  controversies  related  to  how  historians  have 
represented the role of Shaka kaSenzagahkona in explaining changes at this time: 
the debate on the term or idea of Mfecane and the debate on the term or the idea 
of ‘Tribe’.  In doing this, we will explore what kinds of evidence historians use, 
how historical narratives are created and how they are then mobilized in ongoing 
debates about land and authority.  The second case study looks at the cattle-killing 
movement among the amaXhosa in 1856-7, through which we consider diverse 
ways in which events that had a devastating impact on African societies along the 
Cape  coast  can  be  interpreted.  We  begin  by  performing  a  critical  review  of 
contrasting interpretations put forward by different historians, in Xhosa oral and 
written  history,  and  through  the  photographic  depictions  of  Nongqawuse  and 
Xhosa chiefs. We further look at debates about whether or not conspiracy theories 
should be entertained in history.  Across all case studies and quarters of this course, 

 
 
 
 
 
we  are  concerned  with  another  theme:  the  use  of  evidence  and  historical 
interpretation. In this course we will assist you in identifying and understanding 
different interpretations of the same historical events.  By ‘develop’ we mean: to 
assess the value of conflicting interpretations and, most importantly, enable you 
structure  your  own  historical  argument.  So,  the  main  focus  of  the  course  is: 
presenting a structured argument backed up with evidence. 

HISTORY 154 (HIS154) 
History and evidence: Selected themes in African histories from 
the tenth to the nineteenth centuries 

This  course  follows  from  HIS153  in  so  far  as  we  continue  to  ask  that  you 
understand  the  work  of  history  as  narratives  constructed  through  debates  and 
arguments that are backed up with evidence. Our focus in the first semester was 
to assist you to develop a coherent and structured argument. During this semester 
we move on to looking at a second major part of historical writing: backing up 
your argument with evidence. It is often argued that without evidence, there can 
be no history. 

Our debates during this semester are around the nature of pre-colonial African 
political organization and on forms of state in southern, east, central, and west 
Africa. Our focus is on two systems of trade and state formation that connected 
central African societies with the eastern shore of the Indian Ocean (from about 
800-1500), and the western shore of the Atlantic Ocean (from about 1500 -1750). 
In the case of the latter, this was the beginnings of the Atlantic slave ‘trade’. In 
HIS154  we  focus  on  two  specific  forms  of  evidence:  archaeological,  and 
documentary evidence.

Brain & Behaviour  The aim of the module is to introduce students to the

The focus is on Neuropsychology and Cognitive

This module explores developmental theories and examines 
physical, cognitive, moral, social, personality, gender roles,

This module aims to introduce students to the field

Furthermore, students will be introduced to

INTRODUCTION TO THE ECONOMY AND BUSINESS 131 
(IEB 131) & PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT AND 
BUSINESS 131/132 (Man 131/132) 

This module, Introduction to the Economy and Business (IEB131), aims to equip 
students  with  the  fundamental  skills  required  to  engage  constructively  with 
current debates in the field of Management. More specifically, it focuses on the 
South African economy and the business sector. On completion of this module, 
students should be able to: (1) Explain the basic principles of economic theory 
and  its  application  in  the  South  African  economy;  (2)  Understand  the  role  of 
consumers,  producers  and  the  government  in  the  economy  (3)  Describe  and 
evaluate South Africa’s recent economic performance; (4) Describe and evaluate 
the requirements for entrepreneurial success in the South African economy; (5) 
Describe and explain the principles of small business functions and apply them 
to real-world  settings (6) Demonstrate an understanding of the environment in 
which  small  businesses  operate;  and  (7)  Develop  a  business  plan  for  a  small 
business. 

This module, Principles of Management and Business (MAN131), which is run 
in the first semester and MAN132 (which is run in the second semester), aims to 
provide students with an understanding of the basic principles of managing the 
functional areas of a business while taking into consideration the environment in 
which South African businesses operate. The module has three main subthemes, 
namely:  (1)  starting  a  business  (entrepreneurship),  (2)  managing  the  business 
(planning, organising, leading and controlling), and (3) implementing the main 
principles of the functional areas within a business. 

XHOSA LANGUAGE ACQUISITION 111 (XHA111) AND 
XHOSA LANGUAGE ACQUISITION 121 (XHA121) 

The  year's  work  is  divided  into  two  semester-long  modules,  each  carrying  15 
credits:  Xhosa  Language  Acquisition  111  (XHA  111)  and  Xhosa  Language 
Acquisition 121 (XHA121). This course is meant for students who are not Xhosa 
speakers. It has been designed to help students learn to speak Xhosa. Students will 
learn to understand when people speak Xhosa and to speak to them too. They will 
also  learn  to  read  and  write  the  language.  As  they  proceed  with  learning  the 
language, they will also learn about the people who speak this language and about 
their  culture  and  traditions.  What  they  learn  in  this  course  will  enable  them  to 
communicate with Xhosa speaking students on campus and build new friendships. 

 
It will also help develop communication skills to use in the real world outside our 
campus and when they are pursuing their careers. 

DEPARTMENT OF POLITICAL STUDIES (EMS BUILDING, 4th 

FLOOR) 

POL 131 Introduction to Political Studies and International Relations 

POL131 is  offered in the  first semester,  and  students will be required to attend three 
lectures and one tutorial per week. This module aims to familiarise students with the 
fundamental  concepts  and  theories  in  Political  Studies  (generally)  as  well  as 
International Relations, a sub-stream of Political Studies. On completion of this module, 
students should be able to identify and describe the key characteristics of politics and 
the  state  in  a  national  and  international  context  (e.g.  authority,  power,  governance, 
legitimacy,  institutions,  and  sovereignty).  The  first  part  of  the  module  will  focus  on 
domestic politics (e.g. politics that take place or exist within a single state). Students will 
specifically  learn  about  elections,  voting,  political  parties,  democracy,  the  executive, 
legislature, and judiciary, etc. in South Africa. In the second part of the module, students 
will  learn  about  political  issues  and  power  dynamics  that  transcend  state  borders. 
POL131 helps students to understand how states interact with one another, and relate to 
non-state actors at a global level. Part two of the module will also discuss the historical 
evolution of the international state system, the formation of the United Nations, and key 
theoretical approaches to the study of international relations. 

POL 142:  Introduction to South African Politics and Politics of the Environment 

In  the  first  semester  we  covered  a  general  introduction  to  politics  and  international 
relations.  This  semester  we  will  focus  on  South  African  Politics  and  Environmental 
Politics. To lay the foundation to understand contemporary South Africa, we will locate 
the  discussion  within  the  history  and  context  of  British  colonialism  and  the  mineral 
discoveries, apartheid and the transition to democracy. Pivotal to this understanding is 
how race and class are constructed, more importantly, why these categories still endure 
30 years into democratic South Africa. Race engulfs the South African psyche in various 
shapes and forms; the questions raised in this course are why it is so and how does race 
become such a pervasive problem in South Africa. The focus of term 4 will be on the 
impact of capitalism on the natural environment in the South African context. In this part 
of the module, students will critically discuss why we are experiencing an environmental 
crisis, as well as the explanation(s) for it.

LLB ELECTIVES OFFERED IN 2025:  A SHORT INFORMATIVE BLURB 

INTRODUCING THE ELECTIVES ON OFFER IN THE FINAL YEAR LLB.  

ADVANCED FAMILY LAW 431 (FAM431:  SEMESTER 1):    

Advanced Family Law expands upon the principles encountered in the first year of 

your LL.B studies in Family Law 121. While the latter module focused on the law of 

marriage, the consequences that flow from marriage, the different matrimonial 

property regimes and the consequences that ensue upon the dissolution of a 

marriage, Advanced Family Law focuses on specific topics, which are not only 

academically relevant, but practically relevant as well. These include, amongst other, 

domestic violence matters, maintenance applications and mediation. The aim of this 

module is to encourage robust and critical thinking on the part of students and to 

teach students practical skills needed for entry into the legal profession. The module 

is taught on an interactive basis, and students will be required to do class 

presentations and to participate in class discussions on a regular basis. 

ADVANCED CRIMINAL LAW 431 (CRL431: SEMESTER 1): 

Advanced Criminal Law 431 expands upon the fundamental principles of criminal 

law, encountered in Level 2 of the LLB degree. This module is composed of capita 

selecta from the fields of criminal law and the philosophy of criminal law. Some of the 

highly contested topics relate to sex work, euthanasia, and criminal incapacity. The 

topics are studied within the context of international law and the South African 

Constitution, with a strong emphasis on social justice. The basic aim of this module 

is to equip you with an advanced knowledge of the core concepts of criminal law, 

and the historical and multiple perspectives and debates regarding these concepts, 

particularly in the context of fairness and justice. Students are expected to: 

  develop an advanced understanding of the competing approaches to and 

philosophies of aspects of criminal law. 

 
 
 
  explain critically the knowledge of the historical development of aspects of 

criminal law. 

  demonstrate a full understanding of aspects of the current law. 

 

illustrate a detailed knowledge of selected criminal law controversies. 

  analyse critically the competing approaches to aspects of criminal law. 

  construct defence and prosecutorial arguments in relation to contested areas 

of criminal law. 

  demonstrate knowledge of social justice in relation to the rules and values of 

criminal law. 

  Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the inter-relationship between 

criminal law, constitutional jurisprudence, and the discourse of human rights. 

ADVANCED LAW OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE (ACR 412: SEMESTER 1):   

The basic aim of the course is to equip students with an advanced appreciation of 

the general structure and core concepts of the law of criminal procedure. Lectures 

will provide students with critical insights into the Law of Criminal Procedure.  It will 

inter alia: 

• afford opportunities to gain detailed knowledge on selected criminal procedure 

controversies and their application in relation to practical situations, 

• enhance students’ ability to construct defences and prosecutorial arguments in 

relation to contested areas of criminal procedure, 

• encourage an advanced appreciation of the general structure and core concepts of 

criminal procedure, and constitutional jurisprudence and the discourse of human 

rights. 

ADVANCED PUBLIC LAW 431 (ADL431: SEMESTER 1):  

This module touches on aspects of public law, focusing on human rights law. A 

substantial part of the course work focuses on minority rights. The discussion 

 
 
includes the specific legal protections available to persons belonging to minorities 

and the general protections that the regimes of human rights offers to every 

individual irrespective of the group a person belongs to. These include the right to 

equality and non-discrimination, freedom of religion, language right and the right to 

self-determination. The module also introduces the indigenous peoples and their 

rights. As an introductory course, ADL431 allows students to develop awareness and 

understanding of international and regional mechanisms affecting minority rights. For 

more information, contact Prof. Yonatan Fessha: yfessha@uwcac.za.  

ADVANCED LABOUR LAW 431 (LBL431:  SEMESTER 1):   

This module will provide a more in-depth and detailed understanding of various 

topics that were dealt with in the Labour Law 321 module. Additional topics which 

highlight the changes in the world of work will also be introduced.  

Topics will be critically analysed, and students will be expected to form and express 

their own opinions on various issues. The module will be of great value and benefit 

to students who are interested in a career in employment/labour law litigation and/or 

consultation, working for the CCMA, bargaining council(s) or trade union(s), being a 

legal advisor at a corporate firm, working with the International Labour Organisation, 

starting own business, and any other context in which labour law is relevant. 

Students are expected to be active participants in the learning process of this 

module. A weekly class presentation has been introduced in this module and 

students are expected to work in groups to present on assigned cases. 

ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION 431 (ADR431:  SEMESTER 1):   

This module will introduce the student to the world of alternative dispute resolution, 

that is, ways in which legal disputes can be resolved without having to access the 

normal litigation system through our various courts. The module will be of great value 

and benefit in most areas of law where disputes arise and parties are unable to 

come to a mutually acceptable agreement. Since these processes are utilized daily, 

especially in the labour law field, students interested in a career in employment or 

 
 
labour law , working for the CCMA or a trade union, working as a legal advisor at a 

corporate firm, or starting their own business, will greatly benefit from a basic 

understanding of South Africa’s Alternative Dispute Resolution System.  

Students will be exposed to challenges in the existing formal court system and given 

opportunities to discuss solutions to these challenges within the unique historical and 

legal background in South Africa. The role played by the Constitution in transforming 

the right to access dispute resolution forums is central to the module. Another central 

concept is professional ethics. Students will be taught how to engage in ethical ADR 

processes, either as a party to a dispute or as the representative to a party to a 

dispute. This module also includes an historical overview of African dispute 

resolution mechanisms and how this is applied in South Africa. 

CHILD JUSTICE 431 (CHJ431:  SEMESTER 2):   

This course focuses on the history of the development of a separate child justice 

system in South Africa. Child Justice is the subject of considerable guidance in 

international law, which is elaborated at the commencement of the course. 

Thereafter, the influence of international law on constitutional provisions affecting 

child justice and underpinning the Child Justice Act 75 of 2010 is highlighted. 

Constitutional jurisprudence in the sphere of child justice is explored also. 

The various elements of the child justice system as reflected in the Child Justice Act 

follow, with a substantial focus on pre-trial procedures, diversion and the new 

preliminary inquiry procedure. The course, therefore, is useful to those intending to 

apply for a position at Legal Aid South Africa, as children are routinely represented in 

pre-trial and trial procedures under the Child Justice Act by Legal Aid South Africa 

staff. 

As the Child Justice Act is being revised in some respects after a number of years in 

operation, the course will deal to some extent with emerging trends in 

implementation of and ongoing improvements to the youth justice system. The 

course will be of interest also to students with a passion for youth development. 

 
 
CLINICAL LAW 431 (CLN431:  BOTH SEMESTERS):   

Clinical Law 431, an elective course presented to final year law students, is an in-

house clinical model of teaching and requires live – client interaction. The Law Clinic 

is the core service learning facility of the Law Faculty which meets the practical legal 

education needs of the Faculty and helps to provide a well-rounded LLB education 

that the law profession demands. The Clinic also aims to inculcate professional and 

human rights values in students by exposing them to issues affecting indigent people 

and to human rights abuses. Apart from the opportunity of “practicing law”, the Law 

Clinic experience also exposes students to practicing the law within the context of 

diverse racial and cultural groups, and students are encouraged to develop a critical 

approach towards the role of the law and of Attorneys in upholding human rights and 

achieving justice for all. In providing the clinical legal education (CLE) academic 

programme, the Clinic is tantamount to a Law laboratory.  Final year LLB students, 

who are registered for the elective, spend a year in the Law Clinic.   

COMPARATIVE CRIMINAL JUSTICE 411 (CRJ411)  Missouri study abroad 

programme – July holiday):   

This joint course is offered to students from Missouri University and from the 

University of the Western Cape. The module will provide students with an overview 

of the theory and actual practice of certain features of the South African and 

American criminal justice systems. The module is not designed to give students a 

comprehensive understanding of the South African or the American criminal justice 

systems.  Rather, by focusing on certain select topics – the delivery of defence 

services, plea-bargaining, sentencing policies, corrections, and the death penalty – 

our goal is for students to gain an appreciation for how two different systems grapple 

with very similar problems. It will be a comparative module so students will be 

learning about the administration of justice within the South African system while 

also learning about the American criminal justice system. 

 
 
 
 
COMPETITION LAW 431 (CPT431:  SEMESTER 1):   

The  LLB  course  in  competition  law  provides  valuable  insights  into  the  regulation  of 

competition in South Africa, with a particular focus on the critical components of the 

Competition  Act  89  of  1998.  The  course  covers  key  topics  such  as  horizontal  and 

vertical  restrictive  practices,  abuse  of  dominance,  mergers  and  acquisitions,  and 

jurisdiction. It also explores the interplay between competition law and transformation 

in South Africa, addressing important issues like promoting the interests of historically 

disadvantaged  individuals,  supporting  small  and  medium  enterprises  (SMEs),  and 

considering public interest concerns. 

Additionally, the course delves into the economic dimensions of competition law, 

including competition economics and theories, which form the foundation of the 

subject. This is essential for understanding the dynamics between firms in the 

market and the legal frameworks governing their use of market power to prevent 

anti-competitive practices. 

The module also addresses procedural and institutional aspects of competition law, 

providing a holistic perspective. Beyond its practical application and relevance for 

advanced studies in the field, the course enhances your understanding of related 

areas such as contract law, company law, and restraints of trade. This 

comprehensive approach makes the course an indispensable component of legal 

education. 

CONVEYANCING 431 (CNY431:  SEMESTER 2):   

This module introduces students to the basic concepts and procedures of 

conveyancing, with an emphasis on the Deeds Registries Act, the Administration of 

Estates Act and the Sectional Titles Act. The objective of the course is to build the 

skills necessary for conveyancing in practice and to develop a proper understanding 

of the procedures in the Deeds Office and the   transferring of titles to land.  

 
 
The principles relating to sectional titles, mortgage bonds, subdivision of land, estate 

transfers and the endorsement of title deeds are discussed. Constitutional 

jurisprudence in the sphere of conveyancing is explored also. The course will be of 

interest also to students intending to practice in the real estate sector. 

ENTREPRENEURIAL LEGAL PRACTICE 431 (ELP431: SEMESTER 2) 

Entrepreneurial Legal Practice is practical business and corporate law. This elective 

is a master class and will help students feel like lawyers! 

The elective is designed to enhance students’ practical knowledge of business law, 

company law and corporate law theory. It is intended to help students develop the 

practical skills and knowledge they will need as a candidate legal practitioner or 

lawyers advising on business law, in any capacity, or as a business person. The 

course is taught using a blend of engaging lectures and practical exercises includes 

practical focussed on how to incorporate business entities; understanding various 

business processes, commercial transactions and the structuring thereof; drafting 

various corporate transaction documents and negotiation simulations- using real 

world case studies. 

Critical analysis, critical thinking and class participation is essential. 

Classes are held on-line and in-person once a week. 

Assessments are a combination of oral and written assessments (individal and 

group). 

The class of 2024 rated this elective a 9/10. 

ENVIRONMENTAL LAW 431 (ENV431:  SEMESTER 1):   

 
 
The  purpose  of  the  module  is  to  introduce  students  to  the  fascinating  and  rapidly 

developing field of environmental law. In this module, students will be introduced to 

the  definition  of  the  ‘environment’,  including  an  overview  of  the  function,  scope, 

purpose and development of ‘environmental law’ and governance in South Africa. The 

module also covers the legal principles, policies and rules that are devised in order to 

regulate  the  sustainable  use  and  conservation  of  the  natural  resources  and 

biodiversity;  the  planning  of  the  use  of  land  including  the  location  of  human 

settlements; the control of the impact of human activities on the environment; pollution 

prevention; and waste management. These principles and rules of environmental law 

are largely based on a broad spectrum of the philosophical, ethical, religious, social, 

political and economic convictions of humankind in general.  

The  weekly  themes  in  this  module  are  discussed  against  the  context  of  the 

‘Anthropocene’  -  a  geological  period  of  time  during  which  human  activities  have 

caused  unprecedented  changes 

to  Earth’s  climate  and  ecosystems.  The 

Anthropocene  is  increasingly  described  as  a  ‘crisis  of  human  hierarchy,  of  global 

unevenness,  of  deepening  interdependencies,  of  Earth  system  decay,  of  species 

extinction, of temporal inter and intra-species injustices, and of intensifying patterns of 

interrelated  human/non-human  vulnerability’.  The  Anthropocene  also  describes  the 

new  context  in  which  society  must  consider how  we  should deal  with  the effects  of 

global anthropogenic ecological change, including how we think of and structure the 

relationship  between  humans  and  the  planet.  The  Anthropocene  calls  for  the 

reimagining of the conceptual foundations of environmental law and a re-evaluation of 

the composition and effectiveness of existing institutional environmental governance 

structures  and  mechanisms  in  mediating  or  reconciling  the  human-environment 

interface. Accordingly, students will be required to critically evaluate and reflect on the 

adequacy  of  South  Africa’s  current  environmental  law  and  policy  framework  and 

governance structures for fostering sustainable, just and equitable development in the 

context of the current planetary crisis. 

Topics covered in the module include, among others: 

•  Environmental justice 

•  Constitutional environmental rights 

•  Animal rights and welfare 

•  Biodiversity management 

•  Climate change  

•  Pollution prevention 

•  Waste management 

•  Air quality 

•  Environmental jurisprudence  

GENDER LAW 431 (GEN431: SEMESTER 1):  

Students taking this module will be challenged firstly to think about how everyday life 

is touched by gender and secondly to reflect critically on law’s entanglement / 

complicity with gender. Concepts like sex, gender, trans-gender. inter-sex, 

patriarchy, difference, sameness, amongst many others, and the law’s response / 

lack of response to them will be studied. The module will be offered in an inter-

disciplinary manner drawing on popular culture, philosophy and political theory in 

order to get a deeper understanding of the possibilities of gender law. This is an 

intensive writing module and assessment will take place by way of journal entries 

and essays.  

INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS LAW 431 (IBL431: SEMESTER 2):   

International  Business  Law  is  a  course  that  will  require  students  to  think  outside  of 

South  African  borders  and  the  confines  of  South  African  Law.  Students  will  be 

introduced to an international world of law, economics, finance and business. Terms 

such as the WTO (World Trade Organisation), IMF (International Monetary Fund) and 

the World Bank will no longer be foreign concepts. The notion of “imports and exports” 

will no longer sound like a shady business or a cover up for some illegal operation and 

students will know how Foreign Investments take place and how these are regulated. 

After completion of the course students will be able to advise clients on how to trade 

across borders (imports and exports) and how to structure such contracts to safeguard 

themselves against risk of non-payment, etc. Students will be able to assist industries 

in approaching government for protection against unfair trade practices from overseas 

exporters  and  will  be  able  to  assist  governments  in  how,  if  and  when  to  apply  for 

 
 
funding from the IMF or World Bank to assist with financial difficulties or development 

needs.  

The course is taught on an interactive basis, and students will be required to do class 

presentations  in  pre-assigned  groups  and  to  participate  in  class  discussions  on  a 

regular basis. 

INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW 431 (IPL431:  SEMESTER 1):   

The objective of the course is to provide an introduction to intellectual property law 

and to ensure that students understand:  

• 

• 

• 

• 

the basic principles of trademark law and unfair competition;  

the basic principles of copyright law; and  

the basic principles of industrial designs and patent law; 

the protection of traditional knowledge. 

Intellectual Property Law seeks to provide students with an understanding of the 

South African intellectual property system and how it fits into the international 

intellectual property regime. Students are thus introduced to the internationalisation 

of intellectual property; the founding theories relating to Intellectual Property Law and 

the different forms of intellectual property (IP) inter alia, trademarks, copyright, 

patents, designs and indigenous knowledge. The application and/or impact of the 

transformative Constitution to this branch of law is also dealt with. 

With the 4th Industrial Revolution and the advent of the digital era, the protection of 

IP has acquired greater significance than before. This course is perfect for students 

who wish to improve their understanding of intellectual property protection. It is also 

important for all attorneys especially those in commercial law. 

 
 
 
 
INTERPRETATION, TRANSFORMATION AND CRITIQUE 431 (CRI431: 

SEMESTER 2)  

This is a new elective that explores how social transformation can be promoted and 

obstructed by the way law is understood, taught, practiced, and applied by courts. 

The module will be of particular interest to students with a keen interest in politics 

and social justice. We explore various critiques of the status quo and the dominant 

approaches to law in post-apartheid South Africa. The module challenges some of 

the key assumptions behind constitutional law, jurisprudence and statutory 

interpretation. In order to do so, the module takes its cue from what has been 

described as an ‘aesthetic turn’ in South African public law scholarship since the 

mid-1990’s, as well as the call to respond to epistemic injustice. Placing the notion of 

the public / public space at the heart of the investigation, themes such as the Truth 

and Reconciliation Commission; the spatial turn; the pluriverse, democracy, 

deliberation, rationality, imagination and judgment will be studied. This module will 

be assessed by way of continuous assessment. This means that there will be no 

examination. Students will be assessed on a continuous basis throughout the 

semester. This is an intensive writing module with all assessment done by way of 

assignments and essays.   

INTERPRETATION, TRANSFORMATION AND CRITIQUE 431 (CRI431: Missouri 

study abroad programme – July holiday):  

This is a new elective that is presented by way of block teaching during the July 

holiday as part of the University of Missouri (MU) study abroad programme. The 

module is co-taught by lecturers from UWC and MU and the class consists of 15 

students from various universities in the USA and 15 students from UWC. The aim of 

the module is to stimulate interaction between the two groups of students and to look 

at various burning debates in jurisprudence from both perspectives. Placing the 

notion of the public / public space at the heart of the investigation, themes such as 

the Truth and Reconciliation Commission; the spatial turn; the pluriverse, 

democracy, deliberation, rationality, imagination and judgment will be studied. 

Numbers are limited. Students who are interested in taking this module might have 

to follow a special application process.   

 
INTERNET LAW 431 (INT431:  SEMESTER 1):   

Can you be accused of defamation for voicing your opinion on Facebook or Twitter? 

Are  contracts  concluded  electronically  valid?  To  what  extent  are  consumers  who 

conclude contracts online protected? If you are an avid user of electronic media, this 

course should be of interest to you. Since the dawn of the digital era, the world as we 

know  it  has  changed  in  subtle  yet  fundamental  ways.  The  phenomenon  of 

globalisation, the advent of the internet and the subsequent rise of social media have 

created new and interesting problems for our society, not least for lawyers. While the 

legal concerns created by the internet are not new, their scale and the way in which 

they  are dealt  with  have  changed.  It  would be unwise  to  ignore  issues  such as  the 

effect of online defamation and the infringement of privacy laws. Coupled with these 

legal issues are various procedural concerns, such as how one should deal with issues 

of jurisdiction, and the admissibility of digital evidence. For a 21st century jurist, it is 

therefore important to have a firm grasp of the perils, pitfalls and opportunities that the 

internet presents us. 

HOUSING, LAND AND PROPERTY REFORM 431 (LLW431:  SEMESTER 2): 

Since the adoption of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, the 

South African land reform programme has been criticised on various levels, with 

reference to economic drawbacks, political interests and human rights demands.  

From a regulatory perspective, a number of policies and laws have been introduced 

to address the racially inequitable land distribution patterns inherited from the 

erstwhile colonial and apartheid governments. Despite this however, limited progress 

has been made. Vulnerable groups continue to live with insecure land tenure, 

whereas the rural landscape continues to show signs of oppression, unequal farming 

practices and unsustainable forms of governance. 

The module offers a detailed and critical analysis of the land reform programme. It 

also unpacks the right of access to adequate housing. The module also draws on 

 
 
 
property law (as a vehicle for transformative goals) to make meaningful suggestions 

for addressing the problem of landlessness as well as inequitable land and racially 

skewed land ownership in South Africa. 

LAW OF ECONOMIC CRIME (LEC431:  SEMESTER 1):  

The Law of Economic Crime 431 considers the history and contemporary conditions 

which motivate the introduction of legal frameworks to prevent and combat economic 

crimes in both the international and domestic sphere.  The module therefore includes 

the identification and understanding of the various types of economic crimes, 

particularly corruption and money laundering, nationally, regionally and 

internationally, as well as the analyses of the socio-economic and political impact of 

such crime. Conceptual and theoretical perspectives will be analysed and the 

functions and operation of crucial institutions committed to the eradication of such 

crimes will be studied.  Furthermore, the ability to develop recommendations to 

promote the prevention, reduction and eradication of economic criminality will be 

explored. Aspects of asset recovery will also be considered. 

LAW OF INSURANCE 431 (LOI431:  SEMESTER 2):   

The Law of Insurance 431 is a final year elective module that deals with the 

intricacies of insurance policies. From determining whether a policy is valid to 

interpreting problematic phrases in policies, from determining whether a claim will be 

paid out to whether a claim is fraudulent, we cover it all. At the end of the module 

you will have a sound understanding of the ins and outs of insurance policies and 

insurance industry in South Africa. 

LEGAL AND RELIGIOUS PLURALISM 431 (LPL431:  SEMESTER 2)  

The relationship between indigenous African laws, religious laws and human rights 

laws generates controversy in South Africa. This course explains the interaction of 

these legal orders as a problematic product of European colonialism and 

globalisation. The topics include major theories of legal pluralism, the historical 

 
 
 
context of customary and Islamic laws in South Africa, and state regulation of 

indigenous African laws and Muslim personal laws. The course focuses on how 

people adapt their normative behaviour in issues of marriage, divorce, succession, 

ownership, and contract. By highlighting how Muslim personal laws and indigenous 

African laws interact with statutory laws, it promotes critical, independent thought 

aimed at solving conflict of law problems in a rapidly globalising world. It is useful for 

students who plan to practice family law, undertake postgraduate studies, work as 

state law attorneys, or as human rights officers in civil society organisations and 

international bodies such as the United Nations, the African Union, and the Southern 

African Development Community. 

REGIONAL INTEGRATION 431 (EUR431:  SEMESTER 1):   

In 2025 this elective will be offered in a multi-module manner. For February, lectures 

will be on campus during scheduled lecture times on a Tuesday from 09:25 – 11:05.  

There will also be two block lecture periods of 3 hours each on the following two 

occasions: 

Friday 14 February from 13:30 – 16:30 in the Legal Aid Moot Court 

Friday 28 February from 13:30 – 16:30 in the Kadar Asmal Moot Court in the Law 

Faculty. 

For the remainder of the semester, March, April and May, all classes will be offered 

online, during the lecture period via the zoom platform. Participants need to ensure 

that they have sufficient bandwidth to join these sessions with video on. 

Regional integration involves the collaboration of countries within a specific 

geographic area to achieve shared economic, political, and social goals. 

Economically, it expands markets, enabling businesses to thrive and attract 

investment. Infrastructure development flourishes through collaborative projects, 

such as cross-border roads, railways, and ports. 

The African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA) stands as a 

groundbreaking milestone in Africa’s journey toward continental integration. It 

embodies the vision of a continent that is interconnected, economically vibrant and 

 
globally competitive. As Africa’s most ambitious free trade initiative, the AfCFTA lays 

the foundation for a unified market of 54 African states and over 1.3 billion people, 

creating unparalleled opportunities for economic growth, poverty reduction, and the 

collective well-being of its nations. 

The benefits of regional integration also extend to individuals. For example, mutual 

recognition of qualifications across borders can open doors to career opportunities in 

other member states. Imagine pursuing a career with the African Union in Addis 

Ababa, the Southern African Development Community in Gaborone, or the 

Department of Trade and Industry in Pretoria—all with the same ease as working in 

your home country.  

This module invites you to delve into the multifaceted dimensions of regional 

integration, from its economic advantages to its legal frameworks and enforcement 

mechanisms. You will explore how adherence to agreements like the AfCFTA 

ensures that commitments translate into tangible benefits. By understanding these 

dynamics, you position yourself to contribute meaningfully to Africa’s transformation 

as a legal practioner or an excellent platform for furthering your studies at Masters 

level at UWC or elsewhere. 

Join us in shaping a unified and prosperous Africa—one where borders are bridges 

and collective progress is the ultimate goal. Your journey toward making a lasting 

impact on the continent begins here. 

SOCIAL SECURITY LAW 431 (SSL431:  SEMESTER 1):   

Social Security Law 431 is the ideal elective for those students who chose to study 

law in order to assist marginalised and vulnerable people. The module follows on from 

Labour Law 321 and covers the various schemes that provide benefits to people who 

used to work but have lost their income due to contingencies such as unemployment, 

maternity, occupational injuries or retirement. The 2025 cohort of SSL431 students will 

be the first to study the National Health Insurance Act, which may provide students 

who pass the module with a comparative advance.  In addition, the module deals with 

the protection offered by the law to people who never had the opportunity to earn an 

income on their own, such as state grants for older persons, persons with disabilities 

 
and families raising children. Aspects of pension law are covered also. All aspects of 

social  security  law  have  increased  in  importance  in  the  context  of  the  COVID-19 

pandemic, the resultant restrictions, and the persistently high rates of unemployment. 

As our faculty is the only one in the Western Cape offering Social Security Law to LLB 

students,  students  taking  this  elective  may  have  an  advantage  over  students  from 

neighbouring universities when applying for jobs, especially in view of the central role 

of social security  for the poor and marginalised in SA. 

TAX LAW 431 (TXL431:  SEMESTER 2):   

Life has two certainties: death and taxes. They affect us all. Even death is no real 

escape from taxation. Death itself may give rise to taxation, namely, estate duty. 

Indeed, a deceased estate remains liable for income tax on postdeath income 

earned by the estate. Insolvency also provides no relief from taxation. An insolvent 

estate is a ‘taxpayer’ under the tax laws of South Africa. Other juristic persons are 

also not immune to taxation. Thus, companies, close corporations, trusts, clubs, 

associations, religious institutions, political parties and the like are all susceptible to 

taxation (such as, VAT, transfer duty, capital gains tax and dividends tax). This much 

is clear: the tax net in South Africa is cast extremely wide. It is for this reason that the 

field of taxation provides limitless opportunities for work, both in the private sector 

and public sector (such as, the South African Revenue Services and Treasury 

Department). Since every natural and juristic person in South Africa is affected by 

tax, and this likely will remain the position indefinitely, there will always be a need for 

persons with knowledge in tax law. 

Such knowledge makes a student of tax law a more marketable commodity when 

seeking employment. Tax law is renowned for being a specialist field pursued by 

hardworking intellectuals who are unafraid of being challenged. Having tax law as a 

credit on a CV creates such a favourable impression as it speaks to the calibre of 

person concerned. If the foregoing resonates with you, then Tax Law 431 is for you. 

It is a semester course that focuses exclusively on income tax. Historically, it has 

been a stepping stone for students seeking to do post-graduate studies in tax law, 

whether at UWC or elsewhere.

INTRODUCTION 

This handbook contains lots of information about your rights and responsibilities as a student 
in the Law Faculty. It has been written to improve communication between the staff and the 
students, and to clarify expectations. Please read it through at the beginning of the year, and 
refer to it throughout the year. 

Please note that this handbook is intended to supplement and not replace the general 
university rules, most of which are set out in the University’s Calendar. 

You will notice that this handbook contains a large section dealing with writing, researching, 
referencing and plagiarism. As a law student, you will have to research, write and submit many 
assignments  for  credit.  Writing  and  research  skills  are  key  components  of  a  law  student’s 
education. They are also essential for practicing law. You cannot become a good lawyer if 
you cannot research the law and write the necessary legal documents. You will not be able to 
provide  your  clients  with  high  quality  legal  services  if  you  are  unable  to  express  their 
arguments precisely in language which is clear, correct and convincing. Therefore, you must 
try and master the art of researching and writing the law as soon as possible. 

Assignment writing is a problem for many students, either because they plagiarise or because 
they  do  not  reference  their  work  correctly.  Please  read  the  sections  on  referencing  and 
plagiarism very carefully and always refer to them when doing your assignments. 

Remember  always  that  words  and  their  correct  usage  are,  as  Lord  Denning  put  it,  ‘a 
lawyer’s tools of trade’. Other professionals have specialised instruments or machines or 
tools to enable them to do their jobs. Lawyers have nothing but words as their tools! Other 
people’s  lives  or  livelihood  may  well  depend  on  your  ability  to  use  words  correctly  and 
effectively. Therefore, you must aim to become a wordsmith as quickly as possible. 

Use  this  handbook  as  a  companion  to  your law  studies. The  law  is a  weird  and  wonderful 
world. We hope that this handbook gives you some of the help you will need as you wind your 
way through it. 

Read the following quotations carefully: 

WS Gilbert (1836 - 1911) 

‘The law is the true embodiment 
Of everything that’s excellent It 
has no kind of fault or flaw, 
And I, my Lords, embody the Law.’ 

Eighteenth-century English Rhyme 

‘The law condemns the man or woman Who 
steals the goose from off the common But 
leaves the greater felon loose 
Who steals the common from the goose.’

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Each of  these  quotations  says  something  very  important  about  the  nature and  meaning of 
law. Reflect on the above quotations as you proceed through your law studies. Think about 
them carefully and critically as you grapple with the many legal issues which you will encounter 
both as a student and as a professional. 

In the meantime, the Law Faculty wishes you all a very enjoyable, productive and successful 
2025!

Welcome to the UWC Law Faculty! 

The  UWC  Law  Faculty  acknowledges  and  appreciates  your  decision  to  choose  it  as  your 

partner in pursuing a career in law. As Dean, I would like to share with you a few reasons why 

I believe you made a wise choice in choosing this faculty. 

UWC is known for the important role it played in bringing about a democratic South Africa. 

Members  of  the  UWC  Law  Faculty  specifically  played  a  significant  role  in  drafting  the 

Constitution that governs our country today. You will learn more about the Constitution during 

your  studies  as  well  as  its  importance  for  every  field  of  law.  You  will  also  learn  about  the 

important contribution that you can make, with your law degree in hand, in the achievement 

of  the  goals  of  the  Constitution.  The  UWC  Law  Faculty  has  amongst  its  staff  some  of  the 

leading researchers in the country from whom you will have the opportunity to learn about the 

Constitution and its implications for society. 

At the UWC Law Faculty, we strive for excellence and in this regard, we offer both the standard 

law modules and a range of specialised modules – at both undergraduate and postgraduate 

level – which will add to your knowledge and understanding of the law, and which will give 

you  an  edge  in  seeking  employment  after  the  completion  of  your  studies.  The  UWC  Law 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Faculty wants you to be able to take on the opportunities and challenges of the 21st century 

in South Africa and the rest of the world. Many former students of the UWC Law Faculty have 

done so by becoming Judges, Magistrates, Ministers in Government, Law Professors, highly 

successful attorneys and advocates as well as leading figures in the business world. You can 

too - through hard work and dedication. 

The  academics at  the  UWC  Law  Faculty  have  diverse  backgrounds,  but  share  a  common 

commitment to bring out the best in their already bright and talented students. We have the 

task of assisting you to learn about the content of the law, but also to think critically about the 

law currently in place. We hope that through your engagement with your law studies and your 

participation in the sporting, social and cultural opportunities offered at UWC you will become 

increasingly aware of the importance of – 

●  always conducting yourself ethically and with integrity, 

● 

treating everyone with empathy and respect, 

●  showing a concern for those who are marginalized and oppressed by society, and 

● 

taking responsibility where it is called for. 

Use your time at UWC to learn not only about the law, but also about and from others, as well

APPLICATIONS PROCESSES 

1.1 WINTER SCHOOL 

The Faculty of Law (UWC), in conjunction with the University of Missouri offers a selected 
number of final year LLB students an opportunity to enroll in a number of courses during the 
June holidays. 

The courses that have been offered in the past include: 

Courses offered jointly by Missouri/UWC 

●  Comparative Criminal Justice (CRJ411) 
●  Comparative Law (CCR412) 

Students wishing to take part in the winter school must take note of two important things: 

1. The requirements and procedure for applying for these courses; and 
2. The process for getting these courses credited to your academic record 

Students interested in taking part in any of these courses should contact Professor Le Roux 
(Room  206,  2nd  Floor,  Law  Faculty  Building)  for  the  Missouri/UWC  courses.  Information 
regarding eligibility for these courses can also be requested from Professor Le Roux. 

Students  selected  for  the  Missouri/UWC  courses  MUST  register  through  UWC  in  order  to 
have the courses credited to their academic record. 

1.2 INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE 

Being able to spend time in another country, and thus encountering a different 
culture, meeting students from other parts of the world, as well as graduating from a 
foreign university, is an invaluable experience. 

Fortunately, many opportunities exist because the Law Faculty has formal exchange 
agreements with inter alia the following universities: 

● 

● 

● 

● 

● 

● 

Humboldt University (Berlin, Germany) 

Howard University (Washington DC) 

University of Missouri (USA) 

Leiden University (The Netherlands) 

University of Utrecht (The Netherlands) 

Leuven University, University of Ghent (Belgium) 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Faculty is also negotiating agreements with several other universities. 

These agreements usually allow for student exchange, which can be for a research visit, for 
credits, or for a degree, depending on the nature of the agreement. 

If you are interested in overseas studies, you should commence or continue with the study 
of a foreign language (German, French, Dutch) as a non-legal module in your first year 
already. 

If you have a good academic record and are interested in studying abroad, please consult 
the notice boards for any new information. Details of any of the exchange agreements may 
be obtained from the Dean’s office. 

1.3 TESTIMONIALS 

If you apply for a bursary, a new programme of study or a job, you may be asked to provide a 
testimonial or reference. Who should you approach in this regard? 

Lecturers write testimonials for students regularly. However, there is little point in asking for a 
testimonial from somebody who does not know you, so it would be preferable if you would 
please approach lecturers with whom you have had some contact (e.g. those whom you have 
consulted about academic matters). 

It also makes sense to approach a lecturer in whose subject you have done well rather than 
one whose subject you have failed once or twice, as you want your testimonial to present you 
in your best possible light! 

A lecturer with whom you have worked well as a research assistant or as a GT/GLA usually

2.3 FIFTY PERCENT RULE 

This rule is used by virtually all universities, both in South Africa and other countries. 

The rule governs the number of credits a student may be granted for modules completed 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
earlier or elsewhere. In simple terms, a student must complete at least 50% of the modules 
at the university that confer the degree. 

For example, this means that if you are doing an LLB at UWC, you may not get credit for more 
than 50% of the modules prescribed for the LLB at another university. In other words, in order 
to graduate with an LLB from UWC you must complete at least half of the prescribed modules 
at UWC, including the exit modules i.e. 240 out of the prescribed 480 credits. 

The rule also governs the time which a student must spend registered at UWC.

that  there  is  in  fact  a  mistake  before  approaching  the  lecturer.  It  is  obviously  a  waste  of 
everybody’s time to have to deal with a non-existent ‘mistake’. 

The lecturer/GLA who has marked your test/assignment will discuss the answers (‘memo’) to 
the test or the assignment in class. If you take the time to compare your answers to the memo 
you will usually understand why you were given a particular mark. 

Students  regularly  say  that  they  have  ‘written  well’  and  cannot  understand  why  they  have 
performed badly. In this regard, please note that there is often a very big difference between 
what you think is the correct answer and the actual correct answer to a question. 

Remember also that you are given credit only for the correctness and quality of your answers. 
You do not get credit for the effort you have put into the piece of work  – at university hard 
work is assumed! 

Please also note that your mark is determined crucially by whether you have answered the 
question as it is posed, and how well you have done so. Many students tend to write down 
everything  they  know  about  a  topic  instead  of  choosing  the  aspects  which  are  relevant  to 
answering  the  question.  The  result  is  that  often  their  answers  contain  lots  of  irrelevant 
information and superfluous material, which devalue their work. 

You must learn to identify what a question is about and answer it as pertinently and clearly 
as possible. Relevance is fundamental also to the practice of law. Legal practitioners know 
that they cannot waste their clients’ time and money on side issues. Unless they are able to 
get to the point smartly and quickly, their clients will move on to different lawyers smartly and 
quickly! 

If after you have compared your work to the ‘memo’, and you still do not understand why you

independent thought. Student and lecturer are teamed together, under the leadership of the 
lecturer, in pursuit of certain common goals, important amongst which is success at the end

lecturer,  especially  in  a  big  class,  where  difficulties  experienced  by  individual  students

services of the lecturer.

reason, to speak in the classroom. However, it must be remembered that you have chosen a 
field of study which will qualify you to enter a profession where verbal skills will, at one time 
or another, have to be exercised. What better place, then, to practice  than in the classroom? 
More importantly, a thought shared will serve to enrich the entire class. However, should you 
still feel reluctant to speak in the classroom please do not hesitate to consult your lecturer.

discipline and of the university. In doing so, the lecturer has to ensure that only those

himself/herself.

7.1 PLAGIARISM 

A.  What is Plagiarism? 

The Oxford English Dictionary (8ed) 1990 defines the verb ‘to plagiarise’ as follows: 

1 
2 

take and use (the thoughts, writings, inventions, etc. of another person) as one’s own. 
pass off the thoughts etc. of (another person) as one’s own.’ 

In an academic context plagiarism refers to copying, and thereby stealing, someone else’s 
ideas or words, whether that ‘someone else’ is another student or the writer of a book, article, 
judgement, statute or any other published work. 

To copy out someone else’s words in an essay, even if they are just describing the law, also 
amounts to plagiarism. You know that copying the essay of one of your classmates is wrong. 
It is no less immoral to copy an academic’s or a judge’s or a legislator’s words just because 
you do not know him or her. 

Plagiarism is considered to be the worst academic crime and the penalties for a plagiarist 
can  be  very  severe.  The  University’s  rules  tell  us  that  plagiarism  is  a  form  of  academic 
dishonesty and that a student who attempts to obtain credit in a module through dishonest 
means commits a serious disciplinary offence. 

Rule 3.1.1 Academic Dishonesty stipulates as follows: 

“Academic  dishonesty  is  any  form  including,  but  without  being  limited  to  plagiarism,  and 
collusion, cheating in tests, examinations, assignments, theses and research papers, or any 
other such conduct that results in a breach or prejudicial effect on the University’s academic 
integrity.” 

In terms of Rule 3.6 and Rule 3.8 students suspected of committing plagiarism will be reported 
to the Proctor who will refer the matter to a Student Disciplinary Court which will then institute 
an enquiry into the matter. The possible penalties which such Court may impose are listed in 
Rule  3.10.4.2  and  includes  penalties  such  as  exclusion  from  residence  or  the  University, 
expulsion from the University, and forfeiting of your degree or diploma etc. 

Plagiarism is a serious offence.  The Law Faculty enforces the rules against plagiarism 
rigorously. 

B.  Why is Plagiarism a Serious Offence? 

To create or produce a work involves time and effort, often lots of both. It is considered to be 
unfair  and  illegal  to  take  the  products  of  someone  else’s  work  without  paying  for  these 
products or for the work, whether the products are physical property or intellectual property 
(ie ideas). 

Where these products are physical (eg a pair of shoes, a jar of jam, a car), taking them 
without paying for them or the work which produced them is easily recognizable as theft.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
It is not difficult to understand that taking someone’s ideas, or intellectual property, without 
payment or at least acknowledgment, is also a form of stealing and is just as unfair and illegal. 

C.  How can Plagiarism be Avoided? 

The answer is simple: refer to and acknowledge your sources! 
Always!! 

1. Direct Quotation 

If you use the exact words of another, you are quoting directly or verbatim. 
Whenever you use any series of words composed by somebody else, put it in quotation 
marks (inverted commas). Then use a footnote to indicate the source of the quoted words. 

Quotation marks and footnotes separate your own words from the words of other authors. If 
there is no clear distinction between your own words and the words of other authors, then you 
are  going  to  stand  accused  as  a  plagiarist.  Forgetting  to  refer  to  and  acknowledge  your 
sources is no defence against a charge of plagiarism. The only way to avoid all accusations 
of  plagiarism  is  always  to  ensure  that  you  differentiate  clearly  between  what  you  have 
composed and what another person has composed. 

Consider the following sentence: 

‘There is no central legislative body in international law with the power to enact rules 
binding upon all states.’ 

The sentence was composed by John Dugard, a famous international lawyer. It is to be found 
on  page  3  of  the  second  edition  of  his  book  entitled  International  Law:  A  South  African 
Perspective, published by Juta & Co in 2000. 

If you wish to use this sentence in an essay, you must acknowledge and identify it clearly 
as the composition of Dugard, by quoting it and footnoting it. 

You may not use the sentence in any of the following ways: 

●  There is no central legislative body in international law with the power to enact rules 

binding upon all states. Not even the UN can enact such binding rules. 

● 

● 

In my opinion there is no central legislative body in international law with the power to 
enact rules binding upon all states. 

In international law there is no central legislative body with the power to enact rules 
binding upon all states.’ 

● 

It is a well-known fact that in international law there is no central legislative body with 
the power to enact rules binding upon all states. 

●  There is no central legislative body in international law with the power to enact rules 

binding upon all states.1

1  Dugard (2000: 3).

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
All five of the above usages of the sentence composed by Dugard amount to plagiarism. Be 
sure that you understand fully why they are all acts of plagiarism. 

Note that even the last usage is unacceptable because although the sentence is footnoted 
correctly, Dugard’s words have not been placed in quotation marks. This omission gives the 
impression that although the idea is Dugard’s, the words are your own. That is obviously false. 
Both  the  idea  and  the  words  are  Dugard’s and  you  must  indicate  this fact  clearly  by  using 
both quotation marks and footnoting. 

2.2.  Indirect Quotation 

If you do not use the exact words of another author, but rewrite the concept or idea which you 
borrow  in  your  own  words  (paraphrasing  or  summarizing),  then  use  what  you  are  quoting 
indirectly. 
Quotation  marks  are  not  used  for  indirect  quotation  (since  it  is  your  own  composition). 
However, it is still necessary to use footnoting to indicate that you are using somebody else’s 
idea or concept (even though you are not quoting the idea or concept  verbatim). 
Consider the following sentence: 

‘Feminist scholarship uniformly rejects the positivist characterisation of law as a science 
of rules which can be understood apart from its historical origins and from the political, 
social and economic conditions which have given it form and shape.’ 

This sentence was composed by Sandra Berns and is to be found on page 120 of her book 
entitled Jurisprudence, published by The Federation Press in 1993. 

If I wish to quote Berns indirectly, I would do it along the following lines: 

Feminist jurisprudence is anti-positivist, rejecting the idea that the rules of law can be 
separated from their historical, socio-economic and political context.1

1  See Berns (1993: 120). 

Note the following: 

I have reformulated Berns’s sentence in my own words. 
I have not used quotation marks, because they are my own words. 

● 
● 
●  But I have used a footnote indicating clearly that the source of my formulation is Berns 

If you follow the Rules of Referencing (found at the end of this handbook as an appendix), 
you are allowed to ‘borrow’ another person’s words and ideas  - this is acceptable because 
you are not pretending that they are your own. 

Please read the appendix on the Rules of Referencing carefully. 

Please apply the Rules of Referencing whenever you are writing an assignment or an 
essay!!! 

If you do, you will never be accused of plagiarism.

8.2 Black Lawyers Student Chapter (BLASC) 

The Black Lawyers Association Student Chapter (“BLAsc”) is a student formation of the 
well-known BLA. The BLA set its foot in 1976 as a response to unjust and oppressive laws 
of the apartheid era that also excluded black legal practitioners from being admitted as 
attorneys and advocates. Thus, central to the BLAsc student is the commitment to 
activism. The BLAsc defines itself in this era as a vessel that aims to assist law students in 
bridging the gap between academia and practice. This is done through creating job 
shadowing opportunities for students. Furthermore, the BLAsc further educates students 
about the need for transformation of the legal profession so that students are not divorced 
from the struggles of black lawyers in practice. Joining BLAsc unites the student voice, 
ensuring all students are heard through a single, collective voice 

8.3 Federation of African Law Students (FALAS) 

The Federation of African Law Students, founded in Nigeria, is a federation of law students 
from around the African continent. FALAS is an international, non-partisan, and forward-
thinking organisation, founded on the pan-Africanist ideology and dedicated to the creation 
of a united Africa and a common ground. As FALAS at UWC, we strive to promote and 
safeguard the interests of fairness, justice, equity, and equality in Africa while remaining 
unified. Our fundamental goal as a student body is to provide chances for law students to 
bridge the gap, build a network of excellent students who will collaborate towards a 
common future, and guarantee that African students are aware of new realities and global 
practices. We are devoted to developing a new generation of young lawyers who will 
contribute to the legal industry. We consider ourselves as the local hub for law students 
with diverse legal, cultural, and religious backgrounds to learn and lead an integrated legal 
community. We intend to bring African law students together as a common voice to ensure 
the attainment of a better Africa through advocacy. Joining FALAS(UWC) means 
committing to serving in the unity of the African voice, promoting the interests of members 
of the legal profession, and taking pride in the identity, intellectual and moral standing, long-
term vision, and good governance of the Federation of African Law Students.

REFERENCING AND STYLE GUIDE 

Students are required to read their manuscripts very carefully, and to check them carefully against this 
reference guide. 

1 

Style 

1.1 

Type 

Italics are used only for emphasis, for case names, names of journals and titles of books, and for web 
sites and other electronic references. They are also used to indicate paragraphs in legislation, as in s 
34(1)(a). Italics are not used for foreign words. All italics in direct quotations are reproduced, however. 

1.2 

Headings 

Main headings are in caps. (e g ‘1   INTRODUCTION’). 

Subheadings and further sub- divisions are in sentence case (eg 1.1;1.2;1.1.1;1.1.2) 

1.3 

Lists 

Bullet points may be used for any list, and should be used particularly where the list consists of phrases 
as opposed to full sentences. Full sentences should start with a capital letter and end with a full stop. 
Phrases may, however, begin with lowercase and end with a semicolon (and a full stop right at the end 
of the list). 

Lengthy items consisting of whole sentences or several sentences may appear in numbered lists (using 
(a), (i) or whatever seems appropriate). Such items always begin with a capital letter and end with a 
full stop. 

Use ‘first’ (not firstly); thereafter ‘secondly’, ‘thirdly’. 

1.4 

Spelling and capital letters 

Use the ‘s’ form of English spelling: recognise, emphasise, analyse, realise. Students should ensure that 
they use the ‘UK English’ spell check. 

Capital letters are used only where essential, i e in all proper names (South Africa, Constitutional Court) 
and by tradition for a few other things, such as, Act, President (of the country), Parliament and the 
Constitution (in the sense of a particular document; otherwise lower case). 

Capital letters are not used for court, appeal court, judge, judge of appeal, committee, board, council, 
municipality, province, premier, etc. (When in doubt, use lower case.)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
1.5 

Numbers, dates, percentages, currencies 

Use words for all numbers between one and ten and for all approximations (about two hundred years, 
a thousand ways). 

Numbers higher than ten are in figures. All numbers in tables and graphs are in figures. So are ages 
(5 years old), percentages (use the words ‘per cent’ in the text (10 per cent), and only use the figure 
% in tables), and measurements and quantities and amounts (6 cm, 40 km, R5 million). It is advisable 
also to use figures where a lot of numbers appear in a piece, as a consistent style looks better. A space 
(not a comma) is used in large numbers, as for instance in 42 567. Where a ‘rands and cents’ figure is 
used, the cents should be connoted by a dot (R456.45). For other currencies, use US$, ₤, €. 

A sentence should never begin with figures. 

Dates and centuries: on 4 July 1978; in the 1980s (not 1980’s – there is no apostrophe); in the twentieth 
century. 

1.6 

Quotations 

Quotations are reproduced exactly, including all original italics and original punctuation. 

Quotations appear in single quotation marks. Quotations within quotations appear in double quotation 
marks. 

Short quotations appear as part of the text. Long quotations, i e quotations of more than three lines or 
more than one sentence, are isolated from the text by being indented from the margin. It is permissible 
to isolate a shorter quotation for emphasis. 

Whenever a quotation is introduced with a colon, the quotation itself should begin with a capital letter 
(using square brackets  to indicate an alteration where necessary).  If no  colon  is  used, the quotation 
should start with lowercase. Where the quotation begins with a capital letter, the closing full stop should 
normally appear inside the closing quotation mark. But if the quotation forms part of the larger sentence, 
the full stop should appear after the closing quotation mark. 

Ellipses need not be used at the start of a quotation but must be used in the middle and at the end of a 
quotation to indicate missing words. Use three dots for any missing word/s and a fourth dot to show 
any missing full stop. (The placement of the dots indicates where the full stop appeared, so it will be 
… . or   ) 

Square brackets are used for all changes and interpolations.

When a book is referred to, the author/s’ name/s must be given as follows in both the footnotes and 
the bibliography: Smith JD, not John D Smith or Smith John D. 

In a reference the co-authors of any work (book, article, chapter, whatever) take an ampersand: Smith 
& Dlamini. Cite up to three authors: Smith, Dlamini & Pillay. Thereafter use ‘et al’. When referring to 
authors in an ordinary sentence the ampersand is not used: ‘Smith and Dlamini believe that . . .’. 

If the named person is the editor, then the abbreviation (ed) or (eds) must appear after the name. 

Book titles take the title case and appear in italics.

The year of publication must appear in brackets after the title (first editions) or edition. 

The precise page number where the authority was found comes next, if necessary. If the book operates 
by paragraphs or sections (to be connoted by ‘para’), then this will be a sufficient reference. If it is 
necessary to refer to both paragraph/section and page, then do so as follows: para 27 160. This latter

Chapters in books 

Where an author refers to a chapter in a book written by a specific author (most commonly in a book

Orientation Week activities kick off on Monday, 3 February 2025 after the Rector’s Welcome 
and run until Friday, 7 February 2025. Orientation starts at 9h00 each day and ends at 15h30 
(Tuesday-Friday).  

All new first-year, full-time, undergraduate students must attend the 5 day Orientation Programme. 
Attendance is compulsory on all days.  
Orientation Week activities, among others, entail:

Learning portal

transitioning from school to university, 
how school and university are different 

•  Making sense of their timetable, accessing online resources and physical venues and 

preparations for the commencement of lectures, etc.  
•  Creating peer support networks and circles of learning  
•  Study groups prior to the commencement of classes

If you miss the Official Welcome and/or Faculty Welcome on 5 February and arrive on campus between

tour between 10-28 February. 

We have created a dedicated Student Orientation page 
on iKamva and the UWC Student Orientation 2025 
Instagram page to access relevant documents and 
videos which will be accessible during Orientation Week 
and beyond. 

Postgraduate Student Orientation   
In 2025 we continue with our pilot Postgraduate Orientation Programme aimed at assisting new first-
time entry postgraduate students to become familiar with their campus services and resources. 

From 4 February we will communicate with first-time entry postgraduate students to sign up for a half-
day only Postgraduate Orientation session (this is a separate service brought to you by UWC Student 
Development and Support to accompany your Faculty Orientation to improve your knowledge of 
services available on campus). 

This Postgraduation Orientation session will include:  

• 

Introduction to the UWC e-learning portal 
(iKamva) 

•  Online Orientation resources via iKamva page  
•  Tour of Campus and Student Support Services 
•  Group discussions on 'How Postgraduate studies 
differs from Undergraduate studies' and how to 
access the Research Development and 
Postgraduate Support (Masters and PhD 
students) among other. 

Watch your new UWC student mailbox for an invitation! 

For queries about Orientation Week email us at orientation@uwc.ac.za 

The Orientation Team 
UWC Student Development and Support

HOW TO GET HELP FROM

Feeling unsure about academic 
writing and what to expect?

The  Writing  Centre  is  a  free  service  offered  by 
the  University  to  assist  you  with  developing  your 
academic writing skills. Our team of postgraduate 
tutors  provides  personalized  feedback  on  your 
drafts, helping you improve your assignments and 
become a better writer.

OUR SERVICES

	z One-on-One Consultations
Get  personalized  feedback  on  your  drafts  and 
assignments to improve clarity, structure and style.

	z Group Sessions
Have a group assignment? Join a group consultation 
for collaborative feedback.

	z Online Consultations
If you cannot make it to campus, no problem! Book 
a virtual session with our tutors from anywhere.

In addition, we conduct workshops on aspects of 
academic writing on request from lecturers.

Getting writing assistance is easy! You can book a 
consultation with us in one of three simple ways:

 Visit the Writing Centre and book an appoint­

Foreword 

An institution or organisation is measured by the successful 
attainment of the vision and goals it set for itself.

Prof Alan Christoff els started his association 
with UWC as a student and has become one 
of the most respected researchers on the 
continent in the ﬁ elds of 
bioinformatics and 
genome mapping. 
The Director of 
the SA National 
Bioinformatics 
Institute, Prof 
Christoff els was 
awarded the 
SARChI Chair in 
Bioinformatics 

As an academic institution, the 

University of the Western Cape 
(UWC) has set itself the ambitious 
vision of being a vibrant intellectual 
space where people engage in matters of real 
signiﬁ cance at the highest levels of 
competence. In a world where mediocrity is 
often regarded as the norm, it is vitally 
important that we off er examples of true 
excellence and this is what we do at UWC. The 
vibrant intellectual space that we create on 
campus and in our lecture halls off ers an 
invaluable antidote to the culture of instant 
gratiﬁ cation. And, it is within these spaces and 
by emphasising qualities such as 
perseverance, resilience and diligence that we 
are able to give life and form to our vision. In 
essence, by creating the right conditions, we 
are able to translate our vision into a reality.

In this magazine, you will ﬁ nd examples of 
alumni who have accomplished exactly that. 
Their years of study at UWC have helped 
them to achieve admirable levels of 
success in their chosen professions. 
Judge Taswell Papier gained his 
undergraduate law degree from UWC, 
spent decades as a lawyer ﬁ ghting on 
the side of the poor and now is a judge 
of the Western Cape Division of the 
High Court. 

Dr Amin Aman Hagos left his 

homeland to study for a Master of Public 
Health degree at UWC and now occupies 
one of the highest public offi  ces in Ethiopia, 
having been named Minister of Health.

and Public Health Genomics in 2009. 

The articles in 360 Perspectives attest to UWC’s 
intellectual space, which creates opportunities for our 
researchers to engage in matters of real signiﬁ cance at 
the highest levels of competence. 

In this issue, Prof Ben Cousins presents a good example 

of thought leadership in his response to the highly 
contentious issue of land redistribution in South Africa. 
Through the Institute for Poverty, Land and Agrarian 
Studies (PLAAS), Prof Cousins has extensively 
contributed to this debate, including engaging with 
government and directly inﬂ uencing policy direction.

The extent of our inﬂ uence is also determined by the 

relationships that we foster which constitute our 
connections to a wider world, and contribute to one of our 
University’s core enabling goals. The Centre for Humanities 
Research, with its extensive continental and global 
networks, is a prime example of scholarship without 
boundaries. This was very evident at the Consortium of 
Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI) Humanities 
Improvised conference held in Cape Town in August 2017. 
The ﬁ rst CHCI conference held on the continent and hosted 
by the Centre for Humanities Research, the event drew 
humanities’ scholars from across the world.

UWC’s foundation of being resilient and resistant to 
labelling has served the institution and its constituents for 
more than ﬁ ve decades. These qualities are as relevant 
now as they were during the University’s formative years. 
In a 21st-century context, it behoves us to be nimble 

and responsive to new forms of knowledge and 
technology, be they in the terrain of big data or searching 
for solutions to challenges that affl  ict our society. That is 
precisely what makes UWC a place to grow and go from 
hope to action through knowledge.

Professor Tyrone Pretorius
