The poet and graphic novelist Nathan Trantraal has been awarded 
the Jan Rabie-Marjorie Wallace Writers’ Bursary for 2018.

The bursary is named for the painter 

Marjorie Wallace and her husband, 
writer Jan Rabie, who was a member 
of the dissident Afrikaans literary 
circle known as ‘die Sestigers’ (along with 
UWC lecturer and playwright Adam Small). 
The prestigious R400 000 bursary, which is 
administered by UWC and awarded every two 
years, supports excellent writing in Afrikaans. 
It is intended to aff ord the winner a year free 
of ﬁ nancial pressure in which to produce a 
literary work.

In awarding the bursary, the judges said, 
“The content and genre is challenging and 
stands out over the 40 applications. Here is a 
brave voice, one that borders the boundaries 
of literature.”

Trantraal describes his entry into the world 

of comic art and graphic novels as a simple 
act of sibling rivalry.

“I’ve always loved comics, but it was my 
brother, Andre, who made me want to draw 
them. Quite literally, he forced me to draw them 
— he recognised something in my drawings 
that he liked. He was obsessed with them. We 
egged each other on, like little kids daring one 
another to do something stupid, just to show 
how brave they are,” says Trantraal.
Growing up in the complex reality of the Cape 

Flats, where danger is a constant presence and 
anxiety is a natural state of mind, bravado and 
escapism were requirements of survival. Yet, 
while his childhood experiences shaped his 
world view and inﬂ uenced his choice of 
creative medium, he resisted being dragged 
down by his surroundings. 

Trantraal says, “I didn’t want to be a social 
conscience artist, but what we as artists could 
never teach ourselves was the light touch. 
Everything we did carried the marks of 
weakness and marks of woe of the places we 
come from. There was always a shadow 
hanging over it.” 

Among his early inﬂ uences were the 

“glamour and gloss” of American comics and 
ﬁ lms and the Tintin and Asterix comic series. 
He was also drawn to the works of author 
Frank McCourt. Referring to McCourt’s 
description of a boiled egg, Trantraal explains 
how this inﬂ uenced his desire to create. 

“Art can only ever be a mirror. I thought, ‘if 

you’ve been so poor and hungry in your life 
that an egg becomes something that you can 
describe in ways that moves someone, and 
still write a great book, why can’t I?’”

co-writer Andre, are part of a growing trend 
among young artists using the medium of

Professor Richard van der Ross 
1921-2017

The University of the Western (UWC) 

hosted a memorial service at the 
Main Hall in honour of its ﬁ rst black 
Rector, Professor Richard Ernest van 
der Ross, who died in December 2017. Family, 
friends, academics and former colleagues 
came to pay their respects at the service, 
which was jointly hosted by UWC and the 
City of Cape Town. 

The Master of Ceremonies was Dr Franklin 
Sonn, former Rector of the Peninsula Technikon 
and lifelong friend. “Prof Van der Ross was 
truly a great man. He was a people’s person. I 
met Prof Van der Ross when I was 14 years old, 

and he became my mentor,” Dr Sonn said. 

Rector and Vice-Chancellor of the University 

of the Western Cape, Prof Tyrone Pretorius 
said: “We are here to think about his life, roles, 
campaigns and the experiences he had in his 
96 years. It is a life worth celebrating.

“I remember as students, many of us could 
not aff ord to travel home during the holidays 
and had to squat in our residences. Prof Van 
der Ross knew about this but did not have us 
removed. Behind his intimidating presence 
and stern face was a passionate man who 
knew the struggle of poor students and 
understood where we came from.”  >>

Cape Town Water Crisis

The issue that preoccupied the people of the Western 
Cape most throughout 2017 was undoubtedly the 
water supply crisis brought on by the drought.

Experts have warned that, without 

major changes in water supply 
management, the Cape Town water 
crisis may become catastrophic, and 

permanent. The Institute for Water Studies 
(IWS) at the University of the Western Cape 
has been working to identify the multiple 
complexities at play in this crisis and to 
advise on feasible strategies for holistic 
resource management. One of the causes of 
the water crisis is undoubtedly climate 
change (and climate variability) which, 
although implicated in resource shortages 
worldwide, further impedes resource 
management eff orts in that it renders any 
historical models worthless.

In addition to the lack of reliable predictive 

models, a crucial issue with resource 
management is the misinformation 
perpetuated by the media and the public. 
Such misinformation assumes that the 
current water crisis is caused only by low 
rainfall and that suffi  cient precipitation would 
resolve the problem. In fact the availability of 
bulk water is complicated by factors such as 

the diff erence between rainfall in the city and 
in the catchments of the surface water 
reservoirs of the city, cost and limitations of 
water distribution infrastructure for 
desalination water, and socio-political 
concerns with wastewater reuse and 
puriﬁ cation. Population growth and in-
migration increased the strain on the available 
resources and combined with the drought to 
deplete the available water resources.  

The greater demands on the City of Cape 
Town’s resources and infrastructure requires 
further investment to expand supply 
capacity. The costs of the maintenance, 
replacement and expansion of infrastructure 
would normally be funded through the City’s 
revenue streams and through the eff ects of 
economic growth (increased consumption, 
increased tax collection and growth in the 
property rates base). 

However, when the City attempted to 
stretch resources by enforcing restrictions 
to reduce water consumption, private users, 
hospitals, schools and industry invested in 
rainwater harvesting, grey water reuse and

households also found alternative water 
sources or made their use of potable water 
less wasteful. Effectively, the water users of 
Cape Town reduced their consumption of

The City reacted by simultaneously

These changes compound the contradictory 
demands of water resources versus water

vulnerable communities.

Among the costly but unavoidable

Research by the IWS aims to increase the 
understanding of surface water, groundwater

ACT

To give effect to the constitutional right of access to any information  held by the
State and any information that is held by another person and that is required for
the exercise or protection of any rights; and to provide for matters connected
theretith.

RECOGNIZING  THAT—

PREAMBLE

*  the  system  of  government  in  South  Africa  before  27  April  1994,  amongst
others, resuhed in a secretive and unresponsive culture in public and private
bodies which often led to an abuse of power and human rights violations;
*  section  8  of  the  Constitution  provides  for  the  horizontal  application  of  the
rights  in  the  Bill  of  Rights  to  juristic  persons  to  the  extent  required  by  the
nature of the rights and the nature of those juristic persons;

*  section  32(1)(a)  of  the  Constitution  provides  that  everyone  has  the  right  of

access to any information held by the State;

* section 32(1)(h) of the Constitution provides for  the  horizontal  application  of
the right of access to information held by another person to everyone when
that information is  requked  for the exercise or protection of any rights;
* and national legislation must be enacted to give effect to this right in section

32 of the Constitution:

AND BEARING IN MIND THAT—

* the State must respect, protect, promote and  fulfil, at least, all the rights in the

Bill of Rights which is the cornerstone of democracy in South Africa;

* the right of access to any information held by a public or private body may be
limited  to  the  extent  that  the  limitations  are  reasonable  and  justifiable  in  an
open  and  democratic  society  based  on  human  dignity,  equality  and  freedom  as
contemplated in section 36 of the Constitution;

*  reasonable  legislative  measures  may,  in  terms  of  section  32(2)  of  the
Constitution, be provided to alleviate the administrative and financial burden
on the State in giving effect to its obligation to promote and  fulfil  the right of
access  to  information;

AND IN ORDER  TO—

* foster a culture of transparency and accountability in public and private bodies

by giving effect to the right of access to information;

* actively promote a society in which the people of South Africa have effective
access to information to enable them to more fully exercise and protect all of
their rights,

B E IT THEREFORE ENACTED by the Parliament of the Republic of South Africa,

as follows:—

The University of the Western Cape is a national 
university, alert to its African and international context 
as it strives to be a place of quality, a place to grow. It 
is committed to excellence in teaching, learning and 
research, to nurturing the cultural diversity of South

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

Thesis:
A Capability Analysis of academic support of NC(V) students at public TVET colleges in 
the Western Cape

Description:
Sasman applied the capability approach to explicate effectiveness and interconnectedness 
of the academic support given to students at TVET colleges. She made use of evaluative 
and  effective  reasoning  to  determine  how  students’  freedoms  are  enhanced  and  if  free 
agency  is  enhanced  in  student  experience.  She  problematized  the    on-course  academic 
support phase  and found that the constitutive part of development is lacking and that the 
functioning space does not optimalise the productive qualities of students. She contributed 
further by designing an Academic Student Support Framework to converge the efforts of 
functionaries and lecturers in TVET colleges, with a focus on transforming the functioning 
space of NC(V) students in South Africa.

Thesis:
Investigating an incremental implementation of African Language programme: A case of 
two primary schools in South Africa

Description:
This innovative study investigates the Incremental Introduction of African Languages (IIAL) 
program in relation to teaching of isiXhosa in Grade two classes. The thesis speaks to the 
complexity  of  multilingualism  in  South  Africa  where  African  languages  are  often  given  a 
lower  status  than  English  and  Afrikaans.  The  teaching  of  African  languages  as  additional 
languages forms part of this study. The research sought to find the teaching strategies used 
by  isiXhosa  teachers  in  implementing  IIAL  to  multilingual  learners  from  different  linguistic 
backgrounds,  and  the  type  of  support  given  to  teachers  by  the  Department  of  Basic 
Education (DBE) in implementing IIAL. This relatively new program is meant to focus on the 
development of African Languages to accommodate language diversity.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

Thesis:
Re-constituting Ghanaian public university libraries to conform to universal design 
principles to accommodate students with disabilities

Description:
Academic libraries must provide students diff erently-abled information access, independent 
library use and social inclusion. Ten Ghanaian public university libraries were investigated to 
determine conformation to universal design principles as underpinned by the Social Model 
of Disability and the International Federation of Library Associations’ checklist for access to 
libraries  for  persons  with  disabilities.  Findings  revealed  that  most  of  the  libraries  were  not 
universally designed, did not have disability policies and lacked fully accessible facilities, services 
and  resources  required  by  students  with  visual,  hearing  or  mobile  impairments.  The  study 
recommends  redesigning  physical  access  to  university  libraries,  websites  and  catalogues  as 
well as adequate budgets for alternative format resources, assistive technology and training.

ELEANOR MARY FOSTER

Supervisor:  

LINGUISTICS
PROF Z BOCK

Thesis:
We shouldn’t stay in our little bubble…we need to go and swim a bit in other bubbles.  
An exploration of the theoretical, pedagogical and social dimensions of Functional 
Multilingual Learning in a Brussels primary school

Description:
Foster’s linguistic-ethnographic intervention study explores the dynamics, opportunities and 
constraints  of  Functional  Multilingual  Learning  in  a  linguistically  diverse  primary  school  in 
Brussels,  Belgium.  Drawing  on  classroom  observations  and  interviews  with  four  teachers 
and  their  pupils,  she  traces  the  teachers’  moves  between  the  symbolic,  scaff olding  and 
epistemological  functions  of  translingual  practice.  She  shows  how  cycles  of  participation, 
self- and interpersonal positionings give changing meanings to diff erent forms of interaction, 
resulting in a range of discursive strategies which positions pupils as legitimate plurilinguals 
in a new linguistic market. Her research contributes to broader ontological debates about 
the nature of language and social justice in education.

Thesis:
Livestock, grazing and land reform in Matabeleland South, Zimbabwe: Dynamics of 
accumulation and social reproduction

Description:
This thesis examines emerging processes of accumulation and social diff erentiation amongst 
land reform beneﬁ ciaries in southwestern Matabeleland Zimbabwe, where livestock production 
predominates. Adopting an agrarian political economy approach, it provide new evidence on 
land reform and livelihoods in dryland settings. The study also draws on the concepts of non-
equilibrium rangeland  dynamics and high-reliability theory to examine how producers sustain 
herds in highly variable environments. Some beneﬁ ciaries are engaged in ‘accumulation from 
below’ through local production while others ‘accumulate from outside’, using income from often 
off -farm  jobs  or  businesses.  The  thesis  argues  that  future  developmental  interventions  must 
incorporate the ﬂ exible, mobile and opportunistic strategies adopted by farmers in these settings.

Thesis:
Immigrant responses to xenophobia in post-apartheid South Africa: from victims to agents

Description:
The thesis is titled Immigrant Responses to Xenophobia in Post-apartheid South Africa: From 
Victims to Agents: the case of Nigeria. The topic is a critical one. It is an original contribution 
that recasts the targets of xenophobia as active rather than passive transnational actors. The 
study was largely based on interviews with various organisations and associations formed 
by Nigerian migrants in South Africa. It documents mobilisation against xenophobia but also 
shows  how  this  links  back  to  transnational  power  from  below  as  major  South  African 
companies  doing  business  in  Nigeria  have  faced  citizen  protests  in  Nigeria.  The  thesis 
breaks  new  ground  by  analysing  the  problem  of  xenophobia  from  a  global  and  Nigerian 
perspective, highlighting how they have mobilised in transnational defensive networks.

Thesis:
Narratives of Statecraft: The role of mythmaking in deﬁ ning Intelligence in South Africa

Description:
Statecraft is the art of building and managing a state, with a special focus on national and 
international  security.  Intelligence  is  a  key  component  of  statecraft.  The  structure  and 
operation  of  intelligence  agencies  follow  the  logic  of  political  narratives  that  draw  on 
historical myths about the people who reside in and govern a state. Mr Madlala has devised 
an analytical framework for studying the role of mythmaking in political narratives that inform 
the  orientation  of  state  intelligence.  He  has  applied  this  framework  to  the  South  African 
context,  identifying  the  myths  prevalent  in  the  pre-  and  post-apartheid  era  and  how  they 
functioned  to  enable  the  speciﬁ c  manifestations  of  state  intelligence  across  diff erent 
administrations  in  the  country.  Consequently,  his  thesis  not  only  contributes  to  a  more 
nuanced understanding of this case, but also off ers a contemporary analytical tool that can 
be employed critically to investigate the myths guiding intelligence practices more broadly.

Description:
This thesis examined the potential for complementarity between formal and informal social 
programs in Kenya. Using a single country case study, namely, Kenya’s old age grant, Inua 
Jamii 70+, the thesis used qualitative research approaches to explore interfaces between 
formal (FSP) and informal social protection systems (ISP). The ﬁ ndings of the thesis highlight

Description:
This study interrogates the challenges posed by plastic wastes in Nigeria. Based on interviews, 
focus group discussions, and comparative literature review, it argues that Nigeria’s regulatory 
framework  for  waste  management  is  obsolete,  fragmented,  and  unreﬂ ective  of  socio-
ecological  dynamics.  It  identiﬁ es  the  challenges  of  plastic  management,  establishes  the 
fundamental  considerations  in  designing  a  sustainable  and  economically  viable  regulatory 
framework,  and  articulates  actionable  recommendations  that  reﬂ ect  the  interests  of 
government, producers, retailers, consumers, and the environment. Theoretically, it developed 
a combined approach of human behavioural change, extended producer responsibility, and 
sustainable development. All the examiners affi  rmed the thesis makes a signiﬁ cant contribution 
to knowledge on plastic waste management.

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success, 
embodying the true essence of what it means to be a student at UWC.
Your journey to this day has undoubtedly been marked by obstacles, yet your 
resolve  to  overcome  them  has  been  inspirational.  Whether  navigating  the 
complexities  of  remote  learning,  and  the  absence  of  traditional  campus  life, 
you have demonstrated exceptional strength and character.

Today, it is essential to acknowledge not only your hard-earned achievements 
but also the support of your parents, guardians, families, and loved ones. Their 
encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your 
journey. And for that, we extend our deepest gratitude. As 
you begin the next phase of your journey, know that you do 
so with our full support and admiration. 

Always remember, you are equipped with the knowledge, skills, 
and values you need to make a diff erence, no matter where life

how far you can go. Move forward with conﬁ dence and courage,

HEADER

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its ﬁ rst website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the ﬁ rst university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Offi  ce to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff  
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and ﬁ nal Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Inter- and intra-lingual translations of complainants’ police sworn statements: 
A co-construction of a legal text in a South African context 

Description:
The study explores the extent to which sworn statements are translated and co-constructed 
as legal texts, and the implications of such legal texts in as far as access to justice is concerned. 
Drawing on CDA, Narrative Theory and CA, the study speciﬁ cally examines both the micro 
and macro linguistic aspects associated with the SAPS’s current model of record construction. 
Through  analysis  of  data  derived  from  30  audio-recorded  police  interviews,  the  ﬁ ndings 
demonstrate that the system of re-telling and/or translation of sworn statements is not in the 
best  interests  of  justice.  Instead,  it  entrenches  the  domination  of  some  languages  over 
others, perpetuating inequalities in the broader administration of justice, thus substantially 
reducing meaningful access to justice for speakers who have limited understanding of the 
languages of record.

PROF F BANDA

Thesis:
Exploring multimodal literacy practices in language teaching at initial teacher education

Description:
The study explored ways in which language teacher students for initial education at higher 
education institutions can be equipped with multimodal literacy skills to provide eff ective 
teaching  in  a  diverse  and  multilingual  South  African  society.  The  major  ﬁ nding  was  that 
lecturers  and  students  tended  to  concentrate  more  on  technologies,  such  as  iPads  and 
computers than on how various resources such as multilingualism, words, sounds, images, 
graphs,  colours  and  gestures  can  be  eff ectively  used  across  these  devices.  The  study 
concluded with recommendations on how multimodal face-to-face and online teaching and 
learning can be integrated into a seamless teaching and learning experience. To achieve 
this, it is crucial to address existing inequalities in access to eff ective teacher training and 
digital resources.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to the University of the Western Cape’s second graduation ceremony 
of 2023. Congratulations to you and to all who supported you – especially your 
parents, guardians and loved ones.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reﬂ ect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacriﬁ ces  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very ﬁ rst day on campus, your ﬁ rst lecture 
and tutorial. I am sure you can recall your anxiety on that ﬁ rst day. Now, at last, 
you have completed the journey of being a student. But many other new 
journeys  await  you.  They  will  test  your  strength  of  character  and, 
perhaps, your integrity and sense of purpose. They will also 

demand your time and dedication. 

But take the lessons you have learned at this university 
with  you:  remember  when  the  road  became  almost  too 
long, and it felt as if you were ready to give up? You persevered 
and succeeded. You acquired vital skills such as patience, resilience 
and diligence. These will stand you in good stead wherever you go.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and best 

wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

When  we  celebrate  important  milestones  at  the  University  of  the  Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep appreciation because, not so long ago, we did not 
know when we would have the opportunity to gather in person. 

This graduation ceremony, therefore, serves as a reminder of how uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more critical to use moments such as these to reﬂ ect on 
how we did not allow defeatism to set in but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas,  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But here you are, and we salute you. We also thank your 
parents, guardians and loved ones for supporting you 
throughout your academic careers and walking this challenging 
journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and purpose, ready to take on the 
next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS

1960:  The University College of the

‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Intervention strategy to improve PMTCT policy implementation for HIV exposed children 
under-ﬁ ve years in two rural sub-districts in South Africa

Description:
Rural  areas  are  lagging  behind  despite  great  strides  in  decreasing  mother  to  child  HIV 
transmission in South Africa in general.  This study aimed to design an intervention strategy 
to  improve  PMTCT  programme  implementation  for  HIV-exposed  children  in  a  rural  sub-
district  in  North  West  using  intervention  mapping  framework.  Firstly,  diff erent  intervention 
strategies  using  integrative  review,  healthcare  workers’  perceptions  and  their  attitudes 
toward the PMTCT programme, mothers’ perceptions on childcare received at the healthcare 
facility, and their role in preventing the spread of HIV to their children were explored. Using 
the ﬁ ndings, a strategy that included a vision, mission, values, principles, strategy objectives, 
and functional tactics was designed. Two articles have been published.

MULIKAT AYOADE IBRAHEEM

SCHOOL OF NURSING
Supervisor:  
PROF P MARTIN
Co-supervisor:   PROF F DANIELS

Thesis:
Development of a model for support of emotional labour of nurses in tertiary hospitals in Nigeria

Description:
Emotional  labour  by  nurses  reﬂ ects  a  stressful  work  environment  where  services  are 
guarded  by  organization  and  professional  display  rules.  To  cope  within  the  environment, 
nurses use deep acting and surface acting strategies. This study aimed to develop a model 
for support of emotional labour of nurses working in tertiary hospitals in Nigeria. A total of 
312 professional nurses (quantitative) and 50 nurse managers (qualitative) participated in the 
study.  The model was developed using four steps of a theory-generating process. Six main 
concepts namely; patient care; conducive working environment; eff ective communication; 
working conditions; team work and appropriate reactive reactions were used to develop the 
model. The model was evaluated against ﬁ ve criteria for model evaluation.

Thesis:
Development of a measurement instrument to assess the stigma aff ecting people who 
use drugs in the Western Cape

Description:
Prioritising interventions such as harm reduction and instruments to measure stigma towards 
PWUD has been highlighted globally. However, the scarcity of such instruments within the 
African  context  is  pronounced.  This  study  aimed  to  develop  an  instrument  to  assess  the 
stigma  aff ecting  PWUDs.  A  three  phased  multi-design  approach  namely:  an  integrative 
review  whose  resultant  domains  of  stigma  informed  the  interview  process  and  item 
generation  was  followed.  Following  was  a  phenomenological  hermeneutic  design  were 
PWUDs  and  their  service  providers  were  interviewed.  The  instrument  design  and  pilot 
testing  included  a  NGT  with  experts  and  PWUDs,  and  a  survey.  Ultimately,  the  designed 
instrument comprised three sections that measured multiple domain of stigma designed to 
ﬁ t the South African context.

shows  that  almost  80  percent  of  children  under  the  age  of  6  are  aff ected,  and  that

identify DNA aptamers against biomarkers for two highly infectious diseases, TB and Ebola. 
These aptamers are now applied in the fabrication of rapid and cost-eff ective point-of-care 
diagnostic tests. This technology can be used to develop diagnostic tests for other diseases.

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

It is one of the wonderful privileges as Chancellor of the University to see the 
joy and pride on the faces of graduands and their loved ones as they walk 
across the stage to receive their degrees or diplomas.

For the students, that moment is the end of a long journey ﬁ lled with challenges, 
growth  and  successes.  Their  pride  is  shared  by  their  families  because  they 
know the sacriﬁ ces involved to get there. 

Former  President  Nelson  Mandela  is  remembered  for  eloquently  speaking 
about the transformational power of education, which is precisely what UWC’s 
graduation ceremonies signify. Some students will be the ﬁ rst in their families 
to attend and complete university, while others will carry on the traditions of 
their families by attending university.

Graduations testify to the University’s success in playing its part in contributing 
to the knowledge economy by producing a new generation of graduates who 
will enter the world of work in South Africa and beyond and contribute to 

developing the societies in which they are located. 

I applaud you for staying the course and for reaching a 
signiﬁ cant milestone in your lives. Warm congratulations 
on your graduation today!

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

As 2022 draws to a close, we gather for this year’s ﬁ nal graduation ceremony 
to celebrate our students’ academic achievements.

This ceremony is rich with symbolism. It marks the end of years of study for our 
students  and  acts  as  recognition  for  a  job  well  done.  It  also  recognises  the 
individual journeys that students have undertaken to get to this moment, some 
of which might be not only marked by great sacriﬁ ces and struggles but also 
by commitment and determination.

It also off ers those who have supported our students a moment to be thanked 
and to enjoy a shared moment of reﬂ ection on the journeys undertaken.

For us at UWC, graduation ceremonies are proud moments that symbolise the 
path  we  have  walked  with  our  students  and  an  appreciation  that  we  might 
have played some role in preparing them for their futures by imparting values 
and attitudes that will stand them in good stead.

Please join the university community in celebrating the 
achievements of our students and their resilience 
and determination to succeed.

Sincerely,

Thesis:
Conservation and resource-use relations: An analysis of the feasibility of protected area 
expansion in the Western Cape 

Description:
The  study  of  location  and  expansion  of  Protected  Areas  is  both  a  scholarly  study  and  of 
practical concern for conserving South Africa’s biodiversity. The essence of such studies is an 
exercise in resolving conﬂ icts. This discipline embraces a range of techniques from advanced 
computational methods to studies of sociology and participatory methods. This study used a 
mixed-methods  approach  to  examine  the  relationships  between  various  stakeholders, 
adjacent  communities  and  the  Protected  Areas’  resources  and  feasibility  for  expansion. 
Three Protected Areas in the Western Cape were studied to provide critical perspectives on 
the dynamics that inﬂ uence conservation and resource-use relations which in turn provide 
perspectives on Protected Areas’ expansion and the need for site-speciﬁ c considerations.

Thesis:
Development of guidelines for adolescents and parents to increase adolescent

Description:
There are no clear strategies available for parents to improve adolescent involvement in 
physical activity. Using a sequential mixed methods approach with Grade 9 learners from 
ﬁ ve  public  high  schools  in  Mitchell’s  Plain,  physical  activity  status,  level  of  parental

determined. As a result of the data collected, Mrs Cozett developed a framework for the 
guidelines. The ﬁ nal guidelines were presented to adolescents, parents, a panel of experts, 
and  stakeholders  in  communities  for  input,  consensus  and  consolidation.  As  a  result,  six 
guidelines with 52 subcategories emerged. Parents can use these guidelines as a resource 
to support adolescents in increasing physical activity participation.

Thesis:
Fracture resistance of endodontically treated maxillary premolars restored with horizontal 
glass ﬁ ber post an in vitro and ﬁ nite element analysis 

Description:
Root-canal  treated  (RCT)  teeth  are  prone  to  fracture  due  to  lost  tooth  structure  and  invasive 
restorative procedures. Conventional, indirect approaches to restore these teeth require multiple 
clinical visits. This in vitro study tested the strength of a less invasive, direct technique to restore 
RCT premolars, by bonding a horizontal glass ﬁ ber post (HGFP) within a composite restoration 
and tooth. The study was supplemented with 3-dimensional ﬁ nite element analysis to improve 
understanding  of    distribution  of  stress  generated  by  occlusal  forces  and  to  explain  failure 
patterns  of  this  complex  structure.  The  use  of  HGFP  increased  fracture  resistance.  More 
importantly, when a failure did occur, the risk for unfavorable fractures is signiﬁ cantly reduced, 
meaning the tooth is not lost. HGFPs suggest a promising, economical approach for clinical use.

Thesis:
Demarcated hypomineralization lesions: Prevalence, defect characteristics and OHRQoL 
among a subpopulation of Saudi children attending King Khalid University outpatients 
dental clinics 

Description:
Demarcated  hypomineralization  lesions  of  enamel  (DHL)  which  includes  molar  incisor 
hypomineralization  (MIH)  and  hypomineralized  second  primary  molars  (HSPM),  is  a  recently 
highlighted dental issue which causes severe dental destruction and discomfort in children and 
impacts on quality of life. A cross-sectional study was conducted in Abha City, Saudi Arabia, to 
ascertain prevalence, clinical presentation patterns, and possible link between MIH and HSPM. 
Nearly two out of ﬁ ve children presented with MIH on at least one permanent ﬁ rst molar. MIH-
positive participants were twice as likely to develop dental caries and three times more likely to 
develop clinical complications of untreated caries. The oral health-related quality of life of aff ected 
children was signiﬁ cantly lower. Postnatal aetiological variables were more likely to result in MIH.

Thesis:
Kesterite-ampliﬁ ed aptameric nanobiosensors for interferon gamma tuberculosis 
biomarker

Description:
The preponderance of TB disease, particularly in developing countries, has heightened the 
need for rapid-result and easy-to-use diagnostic TB tests. The incorporation of nanotechnology 
has become an elegant approach for the development of smart diagnostic tests for disease 
biomarkers or disease indicators. This is because of the ability of nanoarchitectonic materials 
to  improve  the  sensitivities  of  diagnostic  test  protocols.  In  this  PhD  work,  ultrasensitive 
aptasensor for the detection and quantiﬁ cation of interferon gamma (a TB disease biomarker) 
was produced by using a unique kesterite-ampliﬁ ed DNA aptamer nanotechnology invented 
by  Ms  Uhuo.  The  aptasensor  found  special  application  in  the  determination  of  latent  TB, 
which is diffi  cult to detect with the existing TB tests.

MWCNT cathodes for advanced Li-ion Batteries 

Description:
This  study  was  motivated  by  the  global  need  for  safe  and  economical,  renewable  energy 
storage  systems.  Of  particular  interest  was  producing  novel  nanotechnology-based  LMO 
cathode derivatives. During this study, Shane Willenberg proved that sophisticated ion doping 
and coating with NaSi, FeMg and MWCNT eff ectively improves the energy storage capacity 
and  stability  of  the  battery  cathode  system.  To  demonstrate  the  practical  and  commercial 
potential of these ﬁ ndings, the modiﬁ ed nanocomposites were examined in battery cells and 
exhibited promising electrochemical properties and cycling effi  ciencies. Mr.Willenberg research 
exhibit a direct approach to advancing the intrinsic properties of the spinel cathode materials - 
harnessing the energy-storage capabilities of Li-ion chemistries for emerging next-generation 
applications, speciﬁ cally, transportation via electric (EV) and plug-in, hybrid electric vehicles.

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

HEADER

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s first black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its first website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the first university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
The development of a career management intervention programme for academics in a 
South African Higher Education institution

Description:
The  study  provides  a  comprehensive  theoretical  and  evidence-based  framework  for  the 
career management of academics in all career phases. Through an exploratory sequential 
design, consisting of four phases, the study findings provide understanding of the career 
management challenges and components of an enabling institutional culture to consider for 
academic  career  progression  and  strategy  development.  Six  journal  article  publications 
emanated from the results. This study offers leaders and talent management practitioners in 
the  higher  education  sector  with  factors  to  consider  for  interventions.  This  is  required  as 
they attempt to understand academics’ dynamic and demanding progression.

PROF P BRIJLAL

Thesis:
A critical investigation of factors influencing Ugandan family-owned manufacturing 
Businesses’ Performance

Description:
This study investigated the role of resources and capabilities, entrepreneurial orientation, 
and stewardship on the performance of family-owned manufacturing businesses in Uganda. 
It  adopted  an  exploratory  case  study  research  design.  The  study  revealed  that:  general 
management skills, financial management, marketing management, and technology benefits 
are vital resources and capabilities that enhance the smooth operations of achieving better 
performance  and  sustainability.  Family-owned  manufacturing  businesses  should  have  a 
transparent chain of command to streamline decision-making systems and lines of authority. 
The government should develop and implement SME financing and mobilisation policies, 
labour  management,  subsector  policies,  and  standards  regulation  policies  to  enhance 
business performance.

Thesis:
Applying Living labs in the design of emerging digital platforms- a Higher education case 
study in South Africa 

Description:
Candidate Grové investigated how Living Labs, a co-creation approach, informs the design 
process  of  Emerging  Digital  Platforms  (EDP)  in  an  African  Higher  Education  context.  The 
Emerging Digital Platform Lenses (EDP Lenses) as conceptual model and analytical tool was 
created, refined and validated. Application of the EDP Lenses specifically highlighted the 
vulnerability  of  the  Living  Labs  process  to  the  tensions  and  power  dynamics  created  by 
planetary-scale computation as design context and the emergence of digital platforms as a 
new institutional form. Various mechanisms were identified that lead to the eventual failure 
of emerging platforms, including diluting not only capacity to design, but also freedom to 
design.  The  study  presents  a  comprehensive  set  of  design  heuristics  that  may  improve 
future platform designs in developing world design contexts.

The degree is jointly conferred in collaboration with the University of the Western Cape and 
Vrije Universiteit Brussels.

Thesis:
Essays on financial market development, monetary policy and financial stability in South Africa

Description:
The  thesis  examined  the  dynamic  interactions  between  financial  market  development, 
monetary policy and financial stability in South Africa. Vector error correction, Structural vector 
autoregression  and  Bayesian  vector  autoregression  modelling  techniques  were  used.  The 
findings revealed: 1) a significant impact of interest rate, exchange rate and inflation rate on 
financial markets, 2) a significant impact of shocks in domestic economic activity and global 
economic activity on financial stability both in the short and long term, 3) a long term relationship 
between monetary policy and financial stability. Also, a negative response of financial market 
stability to shocks in interest rates, money supply and systematic risks.

Thesis:
Capital structure and profitability of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in Namibia

Description:
The study examined the relationship between capital structure and profitability among State 
Owned  Enterprises  in  Namibia  for  the  period  2011-2020.  Panel  data  modelling  approach 
was used. The findings revealed: 1) a negative relationship between capital structure and 
profitability,  2)  a  negative  (and  statistically  significant)  relationship  between  financial 
performance and liquidity, 3) capital structure of SOEs is better explained by the Trade-Off 
and the Agency cost Theory, which argue that there are advantages to using debt. However, 
the study recommends that SOEs management need to constantly rebalance the equity and 
debt combination, to ensure that the firms’ capital structure is at optimal levels.

Digital readiness and the adoption of self-service banking technologies in South Africa

Description:
Ntswaki Matlala’s thesis: Digital Readiness and the Adoption of Self-Service Banking Technologies 
in South Africa, developed an e-readiness framework that measures consumers’ adoption of 
self-service  banking  technologies  by  integrating  the  innovation  diffusion  theory  with  the 
technology  readiness  index.  This  was  in  response  to  the  lacuna  within  the  literature  limiting 
marketers’ comprehension of the ever-changing digital banking channels. The study adopted 
quantitative techniques and collected data from 362 banking customers. Results indicate that 
personality has relatively more predictive power than product attributes. This, therefore, suggests 
that value-adding and experience-enhancing relationships together with awareness-promotion 
campaigns should be a bank’s priority.

Description:

Thesis:
Customer loyalty programmes in South Africa: past, present and future trajectories

Description:
Nicole Morrison’s thesis: Customer Loyalty Programmes in South Africa: Past, Present and 
Future Trajectories examines the predictive power of utilitarian, hedonic and symbolic value, 
and customer loyalty on repurchase decisions among FMCG retailers. A quantitative study 
of 272 consumers utilising SEM was designed and revealed that loyalty programme benefits 
and  consumer  attitudes  significantly  influence  repurchase  decisions.  However,  mediation 
tests on the effect of gender on repurchase decisions were observed to be non-significant. 
The implications of the study are that retailers should familiarise themselves with consumers’ 
changing needs and design meaningful sustainable loyalty programmes as well as promting 
their benefits to attract and retain customers.

Thesis:
Job demands and resources of academic employees at higher education institutions 

Description:
Due to the wide array of changes in Higher Education institutions, a need exists to understand 
academic  employees’  job  demands  and  resources.  A  tri-phase  exploratory  sequential 
mixed-methods design directed the research process. Results indicated job demands such 
as publication pressure, overburdened with the load, competing time,  work/home balance, 
complexity  of  student  support,  organisational  politics,  lack  of  mental  health  support;  and 
organisational demands, such as using technology-mediated learning and lack of structural 
resources. Social support, autonomy, meaningful work, and personal support were identified 
as job resources. Finally, results from a pre-experimental job crafting intervention showed 
promising results to reduce demands and increase resources.

Tzaneen Municipality, Limpopo Province, South Africa 

Description:
The thesis examined the stakeholders’ perceptions of corporate governance in the Greater 
Tzaneen Municipality, Limpopo Province. The thesis conceptualised corporate governance 
as  adherence  to  municipal  governance  legislation.  The  research  utilised  a  qualitative 
research  approach;  wherein  a  case  study  was  designed.  Findings  revealed  that  non-
accountable organisational cultures, non-compliance with legislation, political interference, 
cadre  deployment,  lack  of  stakeholder  consultations  and  oversight  negatively  impacted 
corporate governance, and subsequent poor service delivery. The study developed a PACE 
Corporate governance model.

Thesis:
The Cost of gaps in existing food price-stabilising market policies in urban areas for poor 
women and their families: the case of Addis Ababa

Description:
This  thesis  investigates  the  impact  of  food  inflation  and  government  response  programs  in 
Ethiopia.  It adopts feminist economics as a framework to take account of women’s gender-
based privations and other facets of their identities and lived realities.  The study shows how 
women in Addis Ababa are impacted by, and cope with, food inflation in relation to the Public 
Distribution System of basic goods. The findings reveal that time poverty, inadequate education, 
and lack of access to resources are some of the main challenges poor women must overcome.  
Despite  facilitating  access  to  basic  goods  to  its  beneficiaries,  the  PDS  failed  to  meet  their 
specific demands in terms of product characteristics such as quality scale, volume, and time. 
This was attributed to the intervention’s androcentric orientation, relying on the extra time and 
effort provided by women in procuring and cooking food to compensate for its inefficiencies.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

1960:  The University College of the

declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

universities in the Mother City.

training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

PROF F DANIELS

Thesis:
Development of a model for nursing management of postpartum Depression in Edo State, Nigeria

Description:
Postpartum depression negatively impacts the quality of life of childbearing women of all socio- 
economic backgrounds. Mrs Amiegheme conducted a qualitative, exploratory descriptive, and 
theory-generative study to develop a model for nursing management of postpartum depression 
in the Edo State, Nigeria. Professional nurses, medical social workers and clinical psychologists 
were interviewed, and patients’ files were reviewed. The Donabedian structure, process and 
outcome model was used as a framework; and concept, statement and theory synthesis were 
used for the development of the model which highlights the importance of adequate infrastructure, 
competent  patient–centred  care,  a  conducive  work  environment,  healthy  nurse–patient 
relationships and satisfactory knowledge, to ensure improved health and patient satisfaction.

Thesis:
Improving child care institutions’ guideline: Exploring risk factors and mediating role of 
psychological capital between institutional care services and children’s mental health 
status in Ethiopia

Description:
Inadequate parental care is implicated in children’s vulnerability to mental health problems in 
Sub-Saharan countries. Ethiopia has countless children cared for in governmental, religious, 
and community-based organisations. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-method design, 
this study aimed to identify major pushing and pulling factors for Ethiopian children’s admission 
into  childcare  institutions,  while  investigating  the  mediating  role  of  psychological  capital  in 
institutional  care  services  on  children’s  mental  health,  and  resilience  following  emotional 
upheavals.  Childcare  institutions’  psycho-social  services  had  a  positive  direct  effect  on 
institutionalised children’s overall mental health. Existing guidelines tended to prioritize basic 
physical health access and needs services than mental health. Recommended guidelines for 
childcare institutions, include a multi-sectoral collaboration aimed at protecting children from 
adverse psychological outcomes.

Thesis:
Use of Continuous Quality Improvement to improve Prevention of Mother to Child 
Transmission (PMTCT) Programme Performance in Amathole district, Eastern Cape, 
South Africa 

Description:
Oyebola’s  research  was  on  the  use  of  continuous  quality  improvement  (CQI)  to  improve 
prevention  of  mother  to  child  transmission  (PMTCT)  programme  performance  in  Eastern 
Cape,  South  Africa.    The  study  demonstrated  that  developing,  testing,  and  monitoring 
change ideas for CQI are essential for improving and strengthening PMTCT programmes. 
The  findings  also  demonstrated  the  value  of  District  Clinical  Specialist  Teams  (DCST), 
multidisciplinary teams that provide technical support and capacity building through face to 
face,  telephonic  and  video  consultations.  This  study  adds  to  the  body  of  knowledge  by 
describing  how  CQI  and  DCST  teams  compliment  government  efforts  to  ensure  facility 
teams take ownership to improve PMTCT programme quality through change management. 
Lastly, the study highlighted the power of synergy and collaboration. It leveraged available 
resources for effective and efficient programme implementation.

Thesis:
A Decolonial Study of Indigenous Teaching and Learning Methods Of Knowledge transfer 
in Gabon’s Rural Communities 

Description:
This empirical study was based in Gabon, where access to education and forms of knowledge 
are  exclusively  established  on  the  Western  hegemonic  system.  Teaching  and  learning 
methodologies  were  integral  to  the  epistemological  and  ontological  systems  that  can  be 
traced back to the 15th century.  The thesis demonstrated how indigenous knowledge systems 
contribute  to  education  in  rural  informal  contexts.  Decolonial  theory  formed  the  theoretical 
framework.  Findings  highlighted  the  value  of  indigenous  teaching  methodologies  through 
various modes, which include language, music, dance, oral tradition, proverbs, myths, religion 
and elders. Integral to the thesis is the imperative to disrupt colonial perspectives on African 
identity and cultural values.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to the University of the Western Cape’s third graduation ceremony of 
2023. Congratulations to you and to all who supported you – especially your 
parents, guardians and loved ones.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reﬂ ect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacriﬁ ces  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very ﬁ rst day on campus, your ﬁ rst lecture 
and tutorial. I am sure you can recall your anxiety on that ﬁ rst day. Now, at last, 
you have completed the journey of being a student. But many other new 
journeys  await  you.  They  will  test  your  strength  of  character  and, 
perhaps, your integrity and sense of purpose. They will also 

demand your time and dedication. 

But take the lessons you have learned at this university 
with  you:  remember  when  the  road  became  almost  too 
long, and it felt as if you were ready to give up? You persevered 
and succeeded. You acquired vital skills such as patience, resilience 
and diligence. These will stand you in good stead wherever you go.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and best 

wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

When  we  celebrate  important  milestones  at  the  University  of  the  Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep appreciation because, not so long ago, we did not 
know when we would have the opportunity to gather in person. 

This graduation ceremony, therefore, serves as a reminder of how uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more critical to use moments such as these to reﬂ ect on 
how we did not allow defeatism to set in but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas,  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But here you are, and we salute you. We also thank your 
parents, guardians and loved ones for supporting you 
throughout your academic careers and walking this challenging 
journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and purpose, ready to take on the 
next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its ﬁ rst website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving
