We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success, 
embodying the true essence of what it means to be a student at UWC.
Your journey to this day has undoubtedly been marked by obstacles, yet your 
resolve  to  overcome  them  has  been  inspirational.  Whether  navigating  the 
complexities  of  remote  learning,  and  the  absence  of  traditional  campus  life, 
you have demonstrated exceptional strength and character.

Today, it is essential to acknowledge not only your hard-earned achievements 
but also the support of your parents, guardians, families, and loved ones. Their 
encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your 
journey. And for that, we extend our deepest gratitude. As 
you begin the next phase of your journey, know that you do 
so with our full support and admiration. 

Always remember, you are equipped with the knowledge, skills, 
and values you need to make a diff erence, no matter where life 
takes you. Take pride in how far you have come, and have faith in 
how far you can go. Move forward with conﬁ dence and courage, 
ready to shape the future and make your mark in the world.

HISTORIC MILESTONES
HEADER

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its ﬁ rst website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the ﬁ rst university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Offi  ce to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff  
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and ﬁ nal Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to the University of the Western Cape’s second graduation ceremony 
of 2023. Congratulations to you and to all who supported you – especially your 
parents, guardians and loved ones.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reﬂ ect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacriﬁ ces  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very ﬁ rst day on campus, your ﬁ rst lecture 
and tutorial. I am sure you can recall your anxiety on that ﬁ rst day. Now, at last, 
you have completed the journey of being a student. But many other new 
journeys  await  you.  They  will  test  your  strength  of  character  and, 
perhaps, your integrity and sense of purpose. They will also 

demand your time and dedication. 

But take the lessons you have learned at this university 
with  you:  remember  when  the  road  became  almost  too 
long, and it felt as if you were ready to give up? You persevered 
and succeeded. You acquired vital skills such as patience, resilience 
and diligence. These will stand you in good stead wherever you go.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and best 

wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

When  we  celebrate  important  milestones  at  the  University  of  the  Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep appreciation because, not so long ago, we did not 
know when we would have the opportunity to gather in person. 

This graduation ceremony, therefore, serves as a reminder of how uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more critical to use moments such as these to reﬂ ect on 
how we did not allow defeatism to set in but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas,  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But here you are, and we salute you. We also thank your 
parents, guardians and loved ones for supporting you 
throughout your academic careers and walking this challenging 
journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and purpose, ready to take on the 
next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS

DAUDA BIVAN AMOS

ENGLISH
PROF N SITHOLE

Thesis:
Bildungsromane by women writing in Africa and the Diaspora

Description:
The  Bildungsroman  has  from  inception  been  a  male-dominated  genre,  but  a  number  of 
signiﬁ cant  women-authored  novels  written  in  the  20th  century  disrupt  these  established 
patterns.  The  thesis  demonstrates  how  women  authors  of  African  descent  deconstruct, 
reappropriate  and  reimagine  the  Bildungsroman  genre  to  create  space  for  the  self-
actualisation of black women. The thesis employs a critical framework that draws from the 
idea  of  counter-discourse,  as  well  as  feminist  criticism  more  generally.  As  opposed  to 
traditional novels that indulge in male heroic self-actualisation, the thesis argues that woman-
authored Bildungsromane articulate the values of collective female experience and a strong 
sense of empowered sisterhood.

ISHAYA ANTHONY  

Department:  
Supervisor:  

RELIGION AND THEOLOGY
DR L SCHARNICK-UDEMANS

Thesis:
Public pedagogy and the socio-political economy of religious media: A qualitative study 
of the Advent Cable Network Nigeria (ACNN) 

Description:
Scholarly  studies  on  the  religious  media  landscape  in  Nigeria  have  predominantly  given 
attention  to  the  activities  of  Pentecostal  Charismatic  Churches.  Ishaya  Anthony’s  thesis 
off ers  a  fresh  and  exciting  angle  to  the  historiography  of  religion  and  media  in  Nigeria 
through addressing the intersections and imbrications that exist within the religion, media, 
and  education  triad  in  the  context  of  the  medialogical  endeavours  of  the    Advent  Cable 
Network Nigeria (ACNN). Underpinned by the concepts of mediatisation of religion, public 
pedagogy and literacy development, the project found that the work of the ACNN extends 
beyond its religio-theological scope to play an important role in reconstructing ,representing, 
and contesting a myriad of socio-political issues in Nigeria.

LINGUISTICS
PROF Z BOCK

Thesis:
Doing friendship: Storytelling and playfulness in casual conversational discourse 

Description:
Awungjia’s study explores the signiﬁ cance of language practices in nurturing friendships. 
The data consists of naturally occurring conversations between ﬁ ve female friends who co-
host  a  YouTube  channel.  Their  offl  ine  and  YouTube  conversations  were  analysed  using  a 
combination  of  sociolinguistics  and  discourse  analysis  approaches,  drawing  on  a  wide 
range of theoretical frameworks. The analysis reveals how the participants’ conversational 
storytelling and play become sites for world-making as their sense of self in relation to the 
other and the world is continuously and discursively negotiated. Accordingly, friendship is 
presented as a spectrum of multifaceted social relations existing outside the constraints of 
kinship  and  legal  obligation,  dynamically  re-negotiated  in  context,  and  mirroring  shifting 
individual needs and life stages.

NOAH DARKO-ADJEI 

Department:  
Supervisor:  

LIBRARY AND INFORMATION SCIENCE
DR L KING

Thesis:
The readiness in selected academic libraries towards the fourth industrial revolution: 
A comparative study between Ghana and South Africa  

Description:
Disruptive  changes  precipitated  by  the  4IR  have  steadily  revolutionized  the  dynamics  of 
library  services  compelling  libraries  to  embrace  technologies  and  artiﬁ cial  intelligence  to 
stay  relevant.  The  study  assessed  the  readiness  for  the  4IR  in  two  advanced  academic 
libraries each from Ghana and South Africa and was guided by an adjusted model emanating 
from the Socio-Technical Theory and Global Competitiveness Index framework. Data from 
171 library directors, librarians and IT staff  revealed signiﬁ cant awareness of the 4IR and fairly 
equipped technologies and applications, but no explicit strategies. In general South Africa 
performed better than Ghana. The study recommended that embracing 4IR technologies 
should be context-speciﬁ c, and librarians should continue to have a growth mindset willing 
to reskill, and upskill and start thinking about the next revolution disruption.

Thesis:
Pilgrimage walking and spiritual well-being: A case study of a personalised COVID trail in 
Cape Town and its surrounding areas

Description:
The art of walking and speciﬁ cally pilgrimage walking creates many opportunities for hope 
and  healing.  However,  despite  its  attraction  as  a  theme  of  global  interest,  research  on 
pilgrimage  in  South  Africa  remains  scanty.  Hannibal’s  study  addresses  this  dearth  by 
exploring pilgrimage walking as an intervention for spiritual well-being. Her study focuses on 
a personalised COVID-19 trail in Cape Town and its surrounding areas. Featuring a novel use 
of digital technology to conduct participant observation, interviews and autoethnographic 
ﬁ eld work, the study delivers rich ﬁ ndings of participants’ enhanced experiences of spiritual, 
mental  and  physical  well-being.  The  ﬁ ndings  are  upheld  as  relevant  for  the  sustainable 
development goal of promoting healthy lifestyles and well-being for all.

THEODORE RONALD RODRIGUES

Department:

PROF B ANTIA

Thesis:
Scaff olding reading comprehension for engineering students at the Cape Peninsula 
University of Technology – a translanguaging framework

Description:
Mr  Theodore  R.  Rodrigues’  thesis  is  titled  Scaff olding  reading  comprehension  for 
Engineering students at the Cape Peninsula University of Technology – a translanguaging 
framework. He analyses the academic reading experiences of students of Engineering for 
whom  English  is  an  additional  language.  He  does  so  against  the  backdrop  of  previous 
research  on  the  ﬁ rst-year  experience,  throughput  rates  in  STEM  education,  and  the 
disconnect between students’ home languages and the medium of instruction in Higher 
Education. He proposes and evaluates a strategy of scaff olded reading and text production 
anchored  in  translanguaging  theory  and  practice.  ‘Translanguaged  texts’  are  found  to 
improve  students’  reading  comprehension,  decrease  (meta)cognitive  barriers  and 
enhance higher-order thinking skills.

Thesis:
The semiotics of the mosque and its impact on self-perceptions of the feminine body

Description:
Shaikjee’s thesis contributes to the ongoing development of linguistic landscape research 
from focusing primarily on text and signage to looking at semiotic landscapes in relation to 
the body. It does so by investigating how the semiotic landscape of the South African mosque 
inﬂ uences Muslim women’s ideas about their bodies and their feelings of belonging in the 
mosque. Methodological tools included walking interviews with South African Muslim women, 
photographs  of  signage  and  architecture  from  thirty  South  African  mosques,  and 
autoethnographic  narratives.  The  thesis  introduces  to  linguistic  landscape  studies  the 
concepts  of  ‘sign  tonality’  and  ‘preference  organization’,  and  uses  the  analogy  of  the 
‘perlocutionary force’ of signs as a novel way to think about the eff ects signs have on readers.

ﬁ ndings, and all her examiners agreed that she made a valuable and important theoretical 
contribution to the understanding of individual and collective agency as a continuum, rather 
than as discrete processes. Her research revealed the ways in which the market women 
were subject to political power, and the ways in which their agency was seriously constrained 
by political and cultural forces. She showed how the market women nevertheless manoeuvre 
within these constraints to achieve a form of collective power, and thus revealed some of the 
underlying socio-political dynamics in a major informal market in Africa.

Thesis:
Child Protection Responses and Transformative Social Protection in Kenya and South Africa: 
Can social grants improve the well-being of children aff ected by violence and Neglect?

Description:
Irene undertook an extensive qualitative study to ascertain how children in care and care 
givers experience child care interventions in Kenya and South Africa. She also examined 
how front line care workers intervene in cases of neglect and abuse, and use social grants 
in this process. She found that the Kenyan care system can be more punitive of neglectful 
and abusive parents, while the South African system broadly uses a more positive therapeutic 
jurisprudence approach to child protection.  South African child care workers however rely 
heavily on social grants, often neglecting active intervention.  Her examiners commented on 
the  broad  range  of  the  research,  which  was  in-depth  and  transdisciplinary.  Irene’s 
recommendations for transformative, post-colonial child care policies for Africa have been 
published and will make a valuable contribution to the ﬁ eld of child care in Africa.

Description:
Operons  are  sets  of  neighbouring  genes  which  are  co-regulated/co-transcribed  in 
prokaryotes.  These  operons  are  associated  with  drug  resistance  yet  the  collection  of 
operons in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) has not been fully described. Tracey’s thesis 
developed  a  new  operon  predictor  called  COSMO  that  uses  the  ever  increasing  gene

outperformed  existing  methods.  Multiple  linear  regression  analysis  demonstrated  that  a 
traditionally used parameter was the least signiﬁ cant parameter. COSMO was able to predict 
an operon that was never predicted under Rifampicin stress. Access to a full Operon Map of 
Mtb through this work allows researchers to focus on operon targets for the design of more 
eff ective anti-TB drugs against drug resistant strains.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded eff ect is meant to reﬂ ect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

Thesis:
A training programme for nurses on the management of preoperative anxiety and 
information needs of patients in Ashanti Region, Ghana

Description:
Sawan Dankyi investigated the exploration and management of preoperative anxiety and 
information needs of patients in the Ashanti region in Ghana. Using the theoretical framework 
of Deliberative theory and an explanatory sequential mixed method research approach with 
the  following  studies:  participant  observation,  cross-sectional  survey,  and  qualitative 
interviews.    The  study  found  high  levels  of  preoperative  anxiety  which  had  a  signiﬁ cant

surgery  on  patient  medical  and  social  outcomes.  Mr.  Dankyi  developed  a  skills  training 
programme for surgical nurses to improve the assessment and management of preoperative 
anxiety. This thesis add new insight into the importance of improving skills on the exploration

Thesis:
Ethico-political leadership in Public Organizations in Zimbabwe

Description:
The study investigated ethico-political leadership in two Zimbabwe State Owned Enterprises 
(SOEs)  to  explore  why  unethical  activities  perpetuate  and  how  to  stem  the  tide.  Reports

and  their  leadership  was  characterised  by  the  normalization  of  corruption  perpetuated 
through social exchange practices manifested in the neopatrimonial order of legitimation. To 
counter this, the researcher recommends the involvement of all stakeholders in eradicating 
unethical  practices.  The  researcher  also  recommends  indigenous  ethical  standards  and 
political practices that include favourable aspects of neopatrimonialism.

Description:
This thesis explores how political and elite social actors construct social policy problems, 
speciﬁ cally ‘child’ pregnancy and ‘early’ marriage in Zambia. The period of interest is 2012-

Thesis:
Fighting corruption in the energy sector in Tanzania 

Description:
This  study  used  institutional  theory  to  examine  Tanzania’s  readiness  to  overcome  the 
corruption challenge that surrounds the energy sector. It argues that Tanzania suff ers from: 
a lack of sustainable political will to ﬁ ght corruption: a weak prosecution system; and poor 
public  engagement  in  ﬁ ghting  this  vice.  In  the  energy  sector,  anti-corruption  eff orts  are 
undermined by poor public engagement in petroleum governance, hesitancy in decision-
making,  ineffi  cient  transparency  mechanisms,  weak  institutional  capacity  to  manage  the 
sector, and weak corporate anti-corruption compliance mechanisms. Lukiko thus proposes 
the constitutional and operational reform of the national anti-corruption system as well as 
interventions to mainstream anti-corruption across the petroleum industry value chain.

Thesis:
Investigation of the in vitro antidiabetic and neuroprotective eff ects of selected 
Helichrysum species against high monosaccharide-induced toxicity 

Description:
Emerging literature evidence suggests a strong correlation between human hyperglycemia 
and neurodegeneration. Thus, most diabetics are likely to develop sensory, cognitive and 
motor  deﬁ cits  at  an  older  age.  In  his  doctoral  project,  Kolajo  Adedamola  Akinyede  used 
cellular models of diabetes mellitus and neurodegeneration to investigate the antidiabetic 
and neuroprotective potentials of select indigenous South African plants, belonging to the 
genus, Helichrysum. His study results showed that these plants signiﬁ cantly improved cell 
viability, reversed oxidative stress, increased cellular energy production, and glucose uptake 
in  the  treated  cells.  Three  peer-reviewed  papers  have  been  published  from  this  project. 
Further studies are recommended in animal models, with a view for drug discovery.

The  consequence  of  climate-induced  abiotic  and  biotic  stresses  is  excessive  crop  yield

defense responses of plants exposed to combined abiotic and biotic stress factors, are in 
many aspects diff erent from the response induced by an individual stress. In Mihlali’s thesis

Thesis:
The development of targeting nanosystems for the treatment of glioblastoma and 
neuroblastoma tumours 

Description:
Glioblastoma (GB) is the most lethal brain cancer in adults, while neuroblastoma (NB) is the 
most common solid extracranial cancer in children. Treatment of GB and NB remains a major 
challenge due to the semipermeable blood-brain barrier, hence Taahirah’s research focused 
on the synthesis of novel bimetallic gold-platinum nanoparticles (NPs) coated with a scorpion 
venom-derived peptide, to speciﬁ cally target and kill GB and NB cells. The study shows that 
the NPs can be targeted to GB and NB cells causing these cells to die, with minimal damage 
to  normal  cells.  Radiofrequency  treatment,  capable  of  penetrating  the  body,  can  activate 
these NPs resulting in the targeted non-surgical removal of cancer cells in the brain. Further 
studies to leverage this application of the NPs, are underway.

than  their  corresponding  pristine  counterparts.  Her  work  has  been  presented  at  various

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded eff ect is meant to reﬂ ect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success, 
embodying the true essence of what it means to be a student at UWC.
Your journey to this day has undoubtedly been marked by obstacles, yet your 
resolve  to  overcome  them  has  been  inspirational.  Whether  navigating  the 
complexities  of  remote  learning,  and  the  absence  of  traditional  campus  life, 
you have demonstrated exceptional strength and character.

Today, it is essential to acknowledge not only your hard-earned achievements 
but also the support of your parents, guardians, families, and loved ones. Their 
encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your 
journey. And for that, we extend our deepest gratitude. As 
you begin the next phase of your journey, know that you do 
so with our full support and admiration. 

Always remember, you are equipped with the knowledge, skills, 
and values you need to make a diff erence, no matter where life 
takes you. Take pride in how far you have come, and have faith in 
how far you can go. Move forward with conﬁ dence and courage, 
ready to shape the future and make your mark in the world.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS

institutions around the world dedicated

access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s first black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its first website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the first university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Development of an intervention strategy to provide emotional support to nurses caring 
for violent patients in acute wards in psychiatric hospitals in the Western Cape

Description:
Violence experienced by nurses working in acute psychiatric settings has been reported. 
Supportive interventions for nurses to ameliorate the deleterious effect of violence shows 
varying response rates or effectiveness. A three-phased, sequential, multi-method research 
approach was used to develop the re.C.H.A.R.G.E strategy for emotional support of nurses. 
The  components  of  the  strategy  consist  of  stress  reduction  techniques:  mindfulness 
meditation,  debriefing,  yoga  and  relaxation  techniques,  spiritual  support  and  educational 
support. The re.C.H.A.R.G.E. strategy focuses on improving coping skills and enhancing self-
care practices among nurses working in acute psychiatric units. The strategy will improve 
emotional well-being of the nurses experiencing violence in the workplace.

Thesis:
The development of a health care decision making model to improve survival of persons 
with traumatic spinal cord injuries (tSCI) 

Description:
Blake Boggenpoel’s thesis addressed; The development of a health care decision-making 
model  to  improve  survival  of  persons  with  traumatic  spinal  cord  injuries.  The  mandate  of 
healthcare systems is to promote survival of service users. Providing the lack of understanding 
on the influencing factors related to survival in this population, Blake developed a preliminary 
fit-for-purpose decision-making model. To achieve this, Blake conducted a rapid review to 
highlight  candidate  injury  characteristics  and  process  of  care  exposures,  collected 
longitudinal  data  for  three  years  on  these  exposures  and  outcomes,  and  performed  a 
descriptive case series of patients who have unfortunately demised. The preliminary model 
demonstrated sufficient sensitivity and should be further validated for implementation.

Thesis:
Mental health of adolescents in refugee camps in Ethiopia: The development of an 
exploratory model based on trauma, coping and resilience

Description:
Persecution,  conflict,  and  displacement  can  cause  mental  health  problems,  particularly  in 
children and adolescents among refugees. Solomon Danga tested a mental health model to 
understand how coping and resilience mediate the relationship between trauma and mental 
health outcomes, moderated by age, gender, and refugee camp duration. The model shows 
that  coping  and  resilience  were  found  to  be  protective  against  negative  mental  health 
outcomes,  with  camp  duration  having  a  moderating  effect  on  adolescent  refugees.  The 
study  emphasises  the  importance  of  individual,  familial,  cultural  and  social  factors  in 
promoting  and  safeguarding  the  mental  health  of  adolescents  who  have  experienced 
trauma. This study is one of few studies conducted on the mental health of young refugees.

Thesis:
Nurses’ and midwives’ perspective on barriers to quality of care within South Africa’s 
public maternal health services

Description:
Jessica’s PhD is entitled “Nurses’ and midwives’ perspective on barriers to quality of care 
within  South  Africa’s  public  maternal  health  services”.  The  PhD  explores  how  nurses  and 
midwives at three Midwifery Obstetric Units in Cape Town understand what barriers exist to 
offering high quality care within their clinics. The key findings of the study show that barriers 
to quality of care include a range of interconnected factors that range from interpersonal 
relations, lack of resources to socio-economic issues. Reproductive justice was used as a 
framework  to  analyse  the  findings.  This  thesis  concludes  that  research  and  action  that 
involves  nurses  and  midwives  in  participatory  ways,  and  changing  policy  or  resource 
allocation to change the clinic environment in which they work, is necessary.

Thesis:
Development of a nutrient profiling model assessing healthfulness of packaged foods for 
adults in the low-income context of South Africa

Description:
South Africans are daily consuming energy dense ultra processed products that are high in 
nutrients of concern to limit such as sugar, sodium, and saturated fat. However, it is very difficult 
for ordinary citizens to identify unhealthy food products with the information currently available 
on  the  packaging  of  these  products.  Following  an  evidence-informed  process,  a  nutrient 
profile model that identifies unhealthy products high in nutrients of concern was developed 
and tested. The alignment between UPP consumption and products subject to warning labels 
was also assessed. This NPM has now been included in draft labelling regulations to underpin 
front of pack warning labels and restriction of marketing of unhealthy food to children. These 
policies have the potential to support the fight against obesity and NCDs in the country.

Thesis:
Strengthening Families Program (SFP) 10 -14: Developing a guideline of actionable steps 
to follow in cultural adaptation for use in South Africa

Description:
The  Strengthening  Families  Program  10-14  (SFP:10-14)  was  implemented  in  26  cultural 
contexts with fidelity and efficacy. The PhD revealed gaps in the operationalisation of the 
cultural  adaptation  process  for  international  dissemination.  The  PhD  developed  the 
Contextual Adaptation Model and Process Checklist (CAMP-C), a set of actionable steps to 
guide  contextual  adaptation  for  South  Africa.  The  artefact  culminates  from  a  multi-phase, 
triangulated study. The CAMP-C has an expanded theoretical structure and clearly articulated 
operational activities that promote systematic decision-making in and reporting of adaptation 
processes. The electronic format enables flexible use. The CAMP-C represents innovation 
and best practice in adaptation research that is firmly grounded in empirical evidence.

Thesis:
The decentralised drug-resistant TB Programme in South Africa: From policy to implementation

Description:
Waasila  Jassat’s  PhD  explored  implementation  of  a  policy  for  decentralising  drug-resistant 
tuberculosis care from specialised centres to more accessible district health services in South 
Africa.  Through  a  qualitative  comparative  case  study  of  two  provinces,  she  showed  how 
implementation was shaped by variable actor buy-in and competing interpretations of policy, 
resource  constraints,  and  insufficient  integration  into  the  district  health  system.  She  also 
revealed how increasing coverage to poorly capacitated sites compromised quality of care. 
Her thesis concludes with a middle-range theory, asserting that implementation of complex 
and  often  ambiguously  defined  interventions,  unfolding  within  a  complex  system  context, 
requires coordinated strategies across multiple levels; and furthermore, results in a dynamic 
interplay between individuals and organisations, that itself shapes the implementation process.

Thesis:

perceptions towards sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence in low-socio 
economic, urban neighbourhoods, Cape Town: A quantitative study 

Description:
Rinko  Kinoshita’s  research  investigated  key  factors  influencing  the  construction  of  early 
adolescents‘ gender norms, using the socio-ecological model. It explored how unequal gender 
norms may influence early adolescents’ sexual and romantic relationships; knowledge of HIV 
and pregnancy prevention; exposure to peer violence and intimate partner violence; adverse 
childhood  events;  and  depression  symptoms.  She  conducted  a  quantitative,  cross-sectional 
study in low socio-economic suburbs in Cape Town, South Africa, as part of the Global Early 
Adolescent Study conducted in 14 other countries. The study confirmed that early adolescents’ 
construct gender norms through a collective influence of multiple levels of the socio-ecological 
model. The study contributes new knowledge to the field and underscores an urgent need to 
incorporate gender transformative interventions that promote early adolescents’ gender equality.

The provision of interprofessional care and practice is essential to the improvement of health 
care services. In her study, Ms. Africa developed guidelines that incorporate interprofessional 
practice principles into the rehabilitation sector of a primary health care facility. Guidelines that 
serve as an operational framework to ensure that the population receives care that is of high 
quality and centred on the needs of the patient were developed through the use of a multi-
method case study methodology. Findings from the study can be used to encourage patient 
care that is viewed through the lens of interprofessional practice. The results of this research

Thesis:
Guidelines for social work interventions with children affected by HIV and AIDS 

Description:
Children  affected  by  HIV  and  AIDS  are  in  need  of  care  which  is  required  by  law  to  be 
attended to by social workers. Social workers are required to design interventions that will 
protect the rights of children in need of care. Although there are interventions attempting to 
support children affected by HIV, these interventions do not clearly define the role of the 
social  worker.  Nomvuyo  Lukelelo  developed  guidelines  for  social  work  interventions  for 
children  affected  by  HIV  and  AIDS.  Using  an  intervention  mapping  research  design,  two 
phases  were  implemented  to  conduct  the  study.  The  guidelines  have  the  potential  to 
strengthen existing social work intervention methods and provide guidance to organisations 
ensuring their interventions support HIV-affected children, caregivers and communities.

Thesis:

hypertension in an urban township in the Western Cape, South Africa

Description:
The rising burden of Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension on weak public health systems 
in low- and middle-income countries require innovative approaches for disease prevention 
and  management.  Tiny  conducted  mixed  methods  research  in  peri-urban  townships  in  the 
Western Cape to gain in-depth understanding of contextual and environmental factors relevant 
to patient self-management and to explore barriers towards optimal self-management among 
health  care  workers  and  patients  living  with  diabetes  and/  or  hypertension.  The  work  was 
complemented by an evaluation of chronic disease monitoring in the public health sector and 
resulted  in  the  formulation  of  a  patient  informed,  contextualised  self-management  care 
package recommended to policymakers for consideration in the public health sector.

Thesis:
Development of evidence-based context appropriate public policy reform models that 
coherently promote healthy food environments and food consumption patterns in Zambia 

Description:
Mulenga’s  PhD  prospectively  explored  opportunities  for  strengthening  policies  to  better 
address  the  food  environment-related  drivers  of  the  double  burden  of  malnutrition  among 
adolescents  in  Zambia.  She  found  that  Zambian  school-going  adolescents  predominantly 
snacked  on  ultra-processed  food  that  is  rich  in  sugar  and  salt  because  these  were  easily 
accessible  and  cheap  around  their  schools.  She  also  found  that  Zambia  does  not  have 
internationally recommended legislative policy measures that regulate the sale of unhealthy 
food  around  schools.  This  was  confirmed  by  the  nutrition-related  stakeholders  who  also 
perceived  that  the  Zambian  legislative  policy  measures  are  unfeasible.  Hence,  a  need  for 
Zambian policy reforms to prioritize guidelines that regulate the school food environment.

Thesis:
The effects of poor menstrual hygiene management on sexual and reproductive health 
and education outcomes among adolescent schoolgirls in rural Tanzania

Description:
David Ngilangwa’s study focused on the effects of menstrual hygiene management (MHM) 
in rural Tanzania on schoolgirls educational attendance and psycho-social well-being using 
a mixed methods approach. Key results from his quantitative study showed that about two-
thirds of the schoolgirls practiced poor MHM. He also found significant associations between 
poor MHM and school absenteeism, reproductive tract infections (RTIs) and embarrassment. 
Qualitative findings revealed that mothers played a key role in counselling and guiding their 
daughters during their menses, while fathers funded sanitary wear. The study contributes 
new  knowledge  on  the  effects  of  poor  MHM  on  schoolgirls’  absenteeism,  RTIs  and 
psychological impact. The need for policies and interventions to ensure access to adequate 
MHM facilities, education, reduction of stigma and retaining girls in school is vital.

Thesis:
Evaluation of a psychosocial support intervention on adherence and retention in care 
among adolescents on antiretroviral treatment in Ehlanzeni district, Mpumalanga 

Description:
Adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) struggle to consistently adhere to and remain engaged in 
HIV care. Mr Okonji conducted an explanatory mixed methods study to evaluate a psychosocial 
support intervention for ALHIV in Ehlanzeni district, Mpumulanga - that aimed to improve viral 
suppression and retention in care, during the time of the COVID-19 pandemic. In demonstrating 
the success of the intervention, he proposes a biopsychosocial model for ALHIV that includes 
enhanced clinical care, facilitated disclosure of HIV status, peer group support and education 
for improved adherence. His doctoral work produced 7 peer-reviewed journal publications.

Thesis:
Conceptualisation and assessment of mental health wellness of adolescents living with 
HIV and on antiretroviral therapy in the Western Cape province, South Africa

Description:
Adolescence  is  a  period  of  tumultuous  change  and  development  –  both  physically  and 
psychologically. Adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) have the double jeopardy of negotiating 
this  challenging  life-stage,  while  coming  to  terms  with  their  chronic  life-long  condition. 
Maintaining positive mental wellness is key to successfully manage the psychosocial and 
physiological stressors of adolescence and being on HIV treatment. However, relatively little 
measures exist to measure mental wellness of ALHIV in Africa. Ms Orth embarked on an 
epic journey to conceptualize mental wellness for ALHIV, and developed the Salutogenic 
Model of Mental Wellness, which informed the Mental Wellness for Adolescents Living with 
HIV – measure. Her doctoral work produced 8 peer-reviewed journal publications.

Thesis:
Understanding the components of comprehensive maternity protection available and 
accessible to non-standard employees in the Western Cape: domestic workers as a case study

Description:
Maternity protection refers to a set of entitlements for working women during pregnancy, 
childbirth  and  upon  return  to  work,  while  breastfeeding.  Katie  evaluated  the  maternity 
protection  policy  environment  in  South  Africa,  especially  as  it  relates  to  non-standard 
workers. Stakeholders’ understanding of and Western Cape domestic workers’ access to 
maternity protection was also assessed. The findings showed that domestic workers have 
insufficient access to maternity protection, and this can negatively influence breastfeeding 
practices.  Universal  comprehensive  maternity  protection  for  all  working  women  could 
encourage  significant  health,  development,  social  and  economic  benefits  for  current  and 
future generations, especially if an enabling environment for breastfeeding was ensured.

Description:
In her thesis, Exploring the State of Social Work Supervision in South Africa, the candidate 
completed an extensive and in-depth analysis of  the supervision  experience of social workers 
and social work supervisors currently applied in the Department of Social Development (DSD) 
and  in  Non-Governmental  Organisations  (NGOs).  The  research  adopted  a  mixed-methods 
approach. The findings of the study suggest that social work supervision is lacking in areas, 
such as creating structure and providing support. Supervision is not prioritised to enable it to 
fulfil its function. Based on the results of the study, valuable guidelines were developed which 
could improve supervision and service delivery within the welfare sector.

Thesis:
The development of a tool to measure and monitor the rate of recidivism of offenders in 
the Department of Correctional Services in the Western Cape

Description:
Recidivism  is  the  relapse  of  criminal  behaviour  that  results  in  an  individual’s  re-arrest, 
reconviction, and re-imprisonment. Although the estimated recidivism rates are unacceptably 
high  in  South  Africa,  the  management  of  recidivism  is  unclear.  Jerome  Samuels  chose  to 
develop guidelines for managing recidivism in the Department of Correctional Services (DCS) 
in  the  Western  Cape.  Through  a  qualitative  approach,  the  guidelines  were  developed  in  a 
2-phased process. Ten guidelines emerged for managing recidivism, which can significantly 
contribute to the policy and policy implementation and procedures for managing recidivism in 
the  Criminal  Justice  Cluster  and  the  Department  of  Correctional  Services  in  South  Africa. 
These guidelines are a much-needed contribution to the criminal justice system.

drivers in South Africa: a cross-sectional study 

Description:
Derrick’s  PhD  sought  to  identify  suitable  anthropometrical  indices  to  measure  the  risk  of 
Metabolic Syndrome among 20 years and older male minibus taxi drivers operating in the 
Cape  Town  metropole  area.  The  taxi  drivers  had  visible  signs  of  body  fat  accumulation, 
especially around the waist. According to the International Diabetes Federation algorithm, 
70% had Metabolic Syndrome. The results also showed that anthropometrical indices that 
measured overall body adiposities such as the Body Mass Index, the percentage body fat, 
and  the  Clínica  Universidad  de  Navarra-Body  Adiposity  Estimator  (CUN-BAE)  were  better 
predictors of MetS risk among this group of taxi drivers. The cut-off points for these indices 
for detecting Metabolic Syndrome were higher than those recommended by the WHO.

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning

sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud

into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways

PROF M BIMEREW

Thesis:
A Postnatal Home Visitation Implementation strategy for community health nurses to 
improve provision of maternal and child health care in selected districts of Ashanti 
Region, Ghana

Description:
The study assessed the postnatal home visitation care provision to improve maternal and child 
health outcomes in Ashanti Region, Ghana. Expectation Conﬁ rmation Theory (ECT) and the 
Donabedian Model of Quality Care (DMQC) framed and guided the sequential mixed methods 
research process with cross-sectional survey and qualitative interviews. The study identiﬁ ed 
maternal  dissatisfaction  of  CHN’s  communication  skills,  health  education  methods,  cultural 
sensitivity and inadequate competencies. Based on the ﬁ ndings the postnatal home visitation 
implementation strategy was developed to improve the CHNs communication skills, postnatal 
knowledge  and  skills,  and  cultural  competencies.  This  study  will  contribute  signiﬁ cantly  to 
improve provision of postnatal home care and maternal and child care outcomes.

CHERYL MARION BLANKENBERG

Department:  
Supervisor:  

SOCIAL WORK
PROF M VAN DER WESTHUIZEN

Thesis:
Guidelines for a coordinated response to bullying of and among children 
with intellectual disabilities 

Description:
Framed within the bio-ecological systems theory, a convergent parallel mixed methods approach 
was  followed  to  respond  to  documented  vulnerability  of  children  with  mild  to  moderate 
intellectual  disabilities  to  bullying.  Through  a  self-developed  survey  and  individual  interviews 
with children exposed to bullying and their caregivers, the nature of bullying and what is needed 
to prevent and respond to bullying were explored. Focus groups with educators described 
systems and procedures to address bullying, and challenges experienced. Delphi interviews 
with key stakeholders in child protection services identiﬁ ed required interventions by formal and 
informal systems. The ﬁ ndings resulted in a practical guideline for a coordinated response within 
child protection services to prevent and address bullying eff ectively.

Thesis:
The eff ectiveness of front-of-pack warning labels in assisting South African consumers to 
identify unhealthy packaged foods

Description:
Unhealthy foods excessive in energy, saturated fats, sugar and salt are associated with obesity and 
non-communicable  diseases  which  has  been  increasing  drastically  over  the  last  two  decades. 
Makoma demonstrated in a randomised control trial that warning labels were more eff ective than 
two other types of front-of-pack labels in assisting consumers to identify foods containing excessive 
amounts of saturated fat, sugar and salt, and increased their intention to act and avoid these 
products. The development of these warning labels was informed by an extensive exploration of 
the perceptions of mothers of children and those that do shopping for their households. The views 
of ordinary South Africans therefore shaped the design of the recommendations on food labels, a 
policy tool that could be used to convey nutrition information to the South African population and 
help to stem the tide of unhealthy food and obesity related diseases.

use disorders (SUDs). In South Africa, legislation mandates organisational support for these 
individuals.  Studies  show  the  need  for  tailored  programmes,  especially  for  employees  re-
entering work post-rehabilitation, to enhance employee well-being, reduce relapse risks, and 
ultimately improve productivity and satisfaction. Using a qualitative methodological approach, 
Eldene  Braaf  designed  a  comprehensive  three-stage  workplace  support  programme 
consisting  of  three  distinct  phases:  Pre-reintegration,  Reintegration,  and  Care  and  Support 
phases.  This  programme  off ers  a  holistic  bio-ecological  perspective  to  tackle  substance 
misuse, emphasizing continuous care and support to facilitate sustainable recovery.

Thesis:
Predictors of harmful alcohol use and the inﬂ uence of commercial determinants of health: 
A hybrid mixed methods study 

Description:
Excessive alcohol use is a major public health concern in South Africa with a high economic 
burden on the country. Using a hybrid mixed methods study design the COVID-19 alcohol sales 
ban provided an opportunity to explore how the pandemic, online alcohol sales, and illicit alcohol 
sales interacted. Nearly 50% of participants in a Facebook study during the pandemic fell into the 
heavy  episodic  drinking  (HED)  category,  and  the  majority  bought  alcohol  illegally  during 
restrictions.  Newspaper  articles  during  the  same  period  of  restriction  were  predominantly 
unfavourable  toward  the  alcohol  sales  bans  and  focused  mainly  on  the  negative  economic 
impact of the alcohol sales bans whilst indicating government to take responsibility for prevention 
of harmful alcohol use. In slight contrast, a national survey completed post-COVID-19 found that 
South Africans were overwhelmingly supportive of increased strictness of alcohol regulations.

good from the past and build the future.

and creativity.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

Thesis:
An encounter with the structural and spiritual violence of coloniality: Intersectional 
understanding of Black students’ experiences of exclusion in higher education

Description:
This study is a spiritual intervention and decolonial feminist examination of colonial legacies 
that shape Black South African students’ ongoing experiences of discrimination, exclusion and 
marginalisation in the university. Focusing on a group of students who were unable to graduate, 
the study examines how violent institutional cultures and systemic racism, intersecting with 
gender and sexual injustices, undermined their successful academic progress. Collaborative 
work  between  the  researcher,  research  participants,  and  their  collective  ancestors,  has 
produced  an  African  scholarship  which  uncovers  how  coloniality  disrupts  Black  students’ 
spiritual health. The study acts as a prayer for light and celebrates Black students’ resistance, 
victories and the rising up of Black communities amidst colonial violence.

Thesis:
The Buried Chameleon: A Novel and Critical Research Thesis

Description:
The Buried Chameleon is a sophisticated novel, combining multiple story lines across key 
historical periods in SA history from the perspective of numerous characters. It focuses on 
the stories of three women negotiating the complexities of personal and political lives at the 
Cape in the periods of slavery, abolition, and post-1994. It highlights the ambiguity of romantic 
love, which has the power to unite and positively transform, but also to express itself violently 
through  the  desire  to  possess.  The  novel  significantly  adds  to  the  literature  about  Cape 
slavery, connecting the experience of women under slavery with the specific forms taken by 
gender-based violence in contemporary SA. The reflective essay creates a wider context 
through the link with African-American slave narratives.

Thesis:
Rebellious Black Femininities: Embodiments of freedom, desire and agency in 
South African popular culture from 1980 to present

Description:
This study explores rebellious Black femininities articulated through popular culture in South 
Africa from apartheid South Africa in the 1980s to today. The focus shifts from Brenda Fassie’s 
impact in the 1980s to Boom Shaka and Lebo Mathosa during the early years of democracy, 
and on to contemporary women like Khanyi Mbau and the Slay Queen. Their biographies 
articulate rebellious femininities that destabilise hegemonic gendered, sexual and intersecting 
social constructions. The study shows how they do not simply oppose notions of ‘respectable’ 
or ‘traditional’ femininities, but strategically resist dominant norms, while surviving, re-creating 
and co-constructing within heterosexist contexts. Through a biographical, multi-modal and 
critical feminist discourse analysis approach, the thesis explores how rebellious Black women 
model historical and current possibilities for freedom, desire and agency.

PROF T SHEFER

Thesis:
Protesting Death-Disability-Debility Imaginaries: Ontological erasure and the endemic 
violences of settler colonialism 

Description:
This thesis critiques South African Disability Studies’ lack of engagement with racialised structural 
violence, arguing this constitutes ontological erasure and shores up a white epistemology of 
ignorance. In the words of an examiner, the thesis provides a ‘meticulous cataloguing of several 
grievous omissions in Critical (White) Disability Studies that has resulted in the normalisation of 
the death-disability-debility machinery that marks South African Black Life’. Mohamed engages 
with radical violences in South Africa, ranging from gangsterism to land dispossession, to the 
Marikana tragedy, and the contestations of ontological imaginaries in recent decolonial student 
activism. Enriched by narratives from disabled respondents, the thesis argues the imperative to 
understand death, disability and debilitation as endemic to unequal, racial capitalist societies, in 
order to radically shift the onto-epistemic terrain of disability studies.

of difference, Roets’ thesis makes an original contribution to our sociolinguistic knowledge 
of Afrikaans and becoming an Afrikaner today, including an important focus on discourses 
of  empowerment  and  the  benefits  and  costs  of  (re)inventing  new  identities  in  a  post-

Thesis:
A comparative analysis of phonological and morpho-syntactic variations in Lungu, 
Mambwe and Namwanga languages in Zambia 

Description:
The study was an extensive descriptive analysis of Lungu, Mambwe and Namwanga languages 
spoken in Northern Zambia to establish a morpho-phonological and syntactic inventory for 
language documentation and the development of a writing system.  In Lungu, Mambwe and 
Namwanga speaking areas, learners use Bemba, a major African language for initial literacy 
development  before  transitioning  to  English  medium  of  instruction.  Using  elicitation  and 
document analysis methods, it was found that there were more similarities than differences in 
the  three  languages.  The  study  concludes  by  formulating  a  writing  system  for  the  three 
languages in addition to a comprehensive grammar, which writers and curriculum developers 
can use. All these are major contributions to language policy implementation efforts and the 
development of literacy material and for the marginalised groups.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success, 
embodying the true essence of what it means to be a student at UWC.
Your journey to this day has undoubtedly been marked by obstacles, yet your 
resolve  to  overcome  them  has  been  inspirational.  Whether  navigating  the 
complexities  of  remote  learning,  and  the  absence  of  traditional  campus  life, 
you have demonstrated exceptional strength and character.

Today, it is essential to acknowledge not only your hard-earned achievements 
but also the support of your parents, guardians, families, and loved ones. Their 
encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your 
journey. And for that, we extend our deepest gratitude. As 
you begin the next phase of your journey, know that you do 
so with our full support and admiration. 

Always remember, you are equipped with the knowledge, skills, 
and values you need to make a diff erence, no matter where life 
takes you. Take pride in how far you have come, and have faith in 
how far you can go. Move forward with conﬁ dence and courage, 
ready to shape the future and make your mark in the world.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its ﬁ rst website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the ﬁ rst university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Offi  ce to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff  
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and ﬁ nal Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Socio-economic eff ects of the migration policy on foreigners in South Africa

Description:
South  Africa  has  been  a  major  destination  for  migrants  since  1994.  However,  there  have 
been  several  negative  reactions  from  within  leading  to  tensions  between  migrants  and 
locals. Using desktop, qualitative, and quantitative methodologies, this study explores the 
socio-economic eff ects of the migration policy on foreigners in South Africa, off ering insights 
into the social and migration dynamics in the country. Findings indicates that South Africa’s 
immigration laws are negatively impacting immigrants’ integration into society. The resultant 
loss  of  skilled  labor  is  signiﬁ cant,  aff ecting  productivity,  growth,  and  socioeconomic 
development in the system. The South African government must address these issues and 
streamline immigration policies. Three articles from the thesis are currently being reviewed 
by DHET accredited journals indexed by SCOPUS.

CLAUDIA MUKONG

Supervisor:  

INSTITUTE FOR SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
PROF J GOLDIN

Thesis:
An investigation into the attraction, retention and engagement of women in higher 
educational institutions in selected universities in South Africa

Description:
The aim of this study is to investigate attraction, retention and engagement of women working 
in  institutions  of  higher  learning  with  emphasis  on  the  University  of  the  Western  Cape  and 
University of Cape Town respectively. Located within a feminist framework, feminist researchers 
assert that researchers should engage in a critical reﬂ ection of self, power, knowledge, and 
emotion  during  research  process.  A  qualitative  research  design  was  applied  in  order  to 
achieve the aim. Findings of this study indicate that ﬂ exibility in working hours, institutional 
history, teamwork are some of the factors that attract female lecturers to higher institutions.

Description:
The candidate’s doctoral dissertation examines the pivotal management and crisis management 
proﬁ ciencies  essential  for  executive  leadership  within  universities  of  technology.  Conducted 
amidst  the  peak  of  the  COVID-19  pandemic,  data  gathering  necessitated  the  utilisation  of 
online video conferencing, facilitating interviews with 13 executive members representing 
universities of technology. Through meticulous analysis of the amassed data, an extensive 
inventory of management and crisis management competencies emerged. These ﬁ ndings 
promise  substantial  contributions  towards  the  enhancement  of  comprehensive  task 
delineations for the executive cadre in universities of technology, and concurrently harbour 
the potential to inform advancements in skills development initiatives tailored to executive 
management within this academic domain.
