farmers in South Africa

Description:
In  an  era  where  digital  technology  holds  promise  for  transforming  agricultural  practices, 
Smidt’s doctoral research sheds light on the institutional and governance challenges small-
scale farmers face in adopting such innovations. The study proposes a framework for the 
adoption of digital value chains tailored to the needs of small-scale farmers. Smidt validates 
the framework through quantitative and qualitative analysis, culminating in a reﬁ ned model 
that  highlights  the  signiﬁ cance  of  governance  and  institutional  support  in  fostering 
cooperation  among  stakeholders.  Smidt’s  work  off ers  an  alternative  conceptualisation  of 
digital AVC frameworks, providing valuable insights for future researchers, practitioners, and 
policymakers aiming to empower small-scale farmers through digital technology adoption.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s first black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its first website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the first university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Investigating participatory development in South Africa and Nigeria, a case study of 
Stellenbosch and Bwari municipalities 

Description:
This  PhD  thesis  tackles  the  subject  of  participatory  approaches  to  local  development 
through a case study driven approach using Bwari and Kayamandi municipalities in Nigeria 
and South Africa. The candidate uses a qualitative fieldwork driven approach to examine the 
ways  in  which  local  governments  in  the  two  contexts  employ  participatory  techniques  of 
engagement  to  include  communities  in  development  projects  intended  to  empower  and 
capacitate them. Through detailed examinations of the different methods used in the two 
development contexts, focusing on community understandings of participatory engagement, 
The  candidate  has  crafted  a  rich,  detailed  qualitative  methodology  yielding  in-depth 
analytical outputs. Alaji Friday is commended by his examiners for the quality of his data, 
figures and analytical summations of how communities experience participation and their 
perceptions of their impact on development policy making.

THULISILE MBULI 

Supervisor:  

SCHOOL OF BUSINESS AND FINANCE
DR N SIBINDI

Thesis:
The glass ceiling effect in South African companies: an illusion or reality

Description:
Using an ethnography research approach, the study confirmed the changing dynamics of 
the  glass  ceiling  in  South  African  business.    The  progression  of  women  to  position  of 
leadership is slow amidst affirmative actions to promote women into leadership positions in 
the corporate world. To shatter the glass ceiling, the study advances a framework that can 
be used in both private and public sectors.

Thesis:
Employer concerns with the quality of the skills and knowledge of recently employed 
graduates in South Africa: Description, Analysis and Implications for Tertiary Education,

Description:
This qualitative research examined the nature and significance of employer concerns with 
the quality of the skills and knowledge of their recently employed graduates. The research 
focused  on  how  graduates  transfer  their  university  acquired  skills  and  knowledge  to  the 
workplace. Several qualitative data collection tools were employed as well as a review of 
primary and secondary literature sources such as documents and the electronic media. The

The study investigated beneficiary participation in four housing projects in the town of Whittlesea 
in  the  Eastern  Cape.  This  study  makes  an  important  contribution  to  our  understanding  of

understanding of participation in housing projects. Using a qualitative methodological approach, 
the study found that government officials played a dominant role as initiators and executors of 
the participatory process, thus limiting stakeholder participation in the housing projects. The 
study recommends that government involve communities in the formulation of projects from the 
outset in order to ensure active beneficiary participation in the development process.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success,

encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its ﬁ rst website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the ﬁ rst university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Offi  ce to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff  
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and ﬁ nal Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
What does the digital revolution mean for poverty alleviation and inclusive growth in 
Africa? A case study of Ghana and South Africa

Description:
Alex  Boakye  conducted  his  doctoral  research  on  critically  analyzing  the  key  trends  of 
technology in job creation and poverty reduction. The study investigated the dynamics of 
technological changes and explored the diff erent strategies that Africa can use emerging 
technologies to address its fundamental problems of poverty and food insecurity.  In general, 
the study identiﬁ ed major factors for the successful implementation of digital technologies; 
and  developed  an  inclusive  digital  framework  for  promoting  economic  growth  and 
development. His thesis provides suggestions and recommendations as well as alternative 
policy options in South Africa and Ghana.

PROF M DINBABO

Thesis:
A Conceptual Framework for Eff ective Local Integration of Refugees in South Africa: 
Case Study of the Western Cape Province

Description:
The doctoral research study of Mr Albert Mpazayabo focused on developing a conceptual 
framework that seeks to off er pathways for eff ective local integration of refugees in South 
Africa.  The  research  was  contextualised  within  the  selected  theoretical  and  conceptual 
frameworks.  Using  diff erent  types  of  models  and  qualitative  inductive  reasoning,  the 
candidate critically assessed the opportunities, challenges and constraints of integration of 
refugees  in  South  Africa.  His  thesis  provides  recommendations  and  alternative  policy 
options for the integration of refugees in South Africa. The dissertation was produced with 
immense attention to detail and resulted in sophisticated work at the PhD level.

Thesis:
Developing a cybersecurity framework for commercial banks in South  Africa

Description:
The  study  proposed  a  conceptual  framework  for  South  African  commercial  bans  as  direct 
response to the exponential rise of cyber-attacks and threats. It proposed this framework by 
identifying  the  factors  impeding  commercial  banks  from  developing  their  own  frameworks. 
The factors were identiﬁ ed using a mixed methods approach, with qualitative data collection 
facilitated through interviews and quantitative data collected by means of a survey distributed 
to IT, risk, compliance, and governance professionals in commercial banks. The seven factors 
were  less  investment  in  cybersecurity,  lack  of  training  and  awareness,  weak  policies  on 
cybersecurity, outdated governance and management policies and a complex cybersecurity 
environment.  The  study  proposed  that  the  stronger  the  coherence  among  the  identiﬁ ed 
factors is, the better commercial banks are able to defend themselves from cybercriminals.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded eff ect is meant to reﬂ ect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s first black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its first website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the first university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Commercial baby food: Sugar content, consumption and labelling practices in Uganda

Description:
The  nutrition  transition  in  sub-Saharan  Africa  has  increased  consumption  of  processed 
foods in infancy, especially sweetened foods. This has increased risk for nutrition-related 
NCDs, including dental caries, overweight/obesity, and promotes poor food choices later in 
life. Two cross-sectional studies investigated the consumption patterns of a 6-36-month-old 
urban population, the sugar content, and adherence to label guidelines of commercial baby 
foods  in  Uganda.  Most  children  consumed  processed  foods  very  frequently,  which  was 
associated  with  maternal  education  level.  82%  of  baby  foods  had  added  sugar  in  high 
amounts, with only 29% adhering to label recommendations. None of the baby foods tested 
fulfilled both label and nutritional requirements on sugar content. There is an urgent need to 
reinforce Ugandan food regulations and policies and to build strong nutritional education 
programmes  to  create  health-promoting  environments  that  promote  optimal  infant  and 
young child nutrition.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR

SUB-HEADER

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success, 
embodying the true essence of what it means to be a student at UWC.
Your journey to this day has undoubtedly been marked by obstacles, yet your 
resolve  to  overcome  them  has  been  inspirational.  Whether  navigating  the 
complexities  of  remote  learning,  and  the  absence  of  traditional  campus  life, 
you have demonstrated exceptional strength and character.

Today, it is essential to acknowledge not only your hard-earned achievements 
but also the support of your parents, guardians, families, and loved ones. Their 
encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your 
journey. And for that, we extend our deepest gratitude. As 
you begin the next phase of your journey, know that you do 
so with our full support and admiration. 

Always remember, you are equipped with the knowledge, skills, 
and values you need to make a diff erence, no matter where life 
takes you. Take pride in how far you have come, and have faith in 
how far you can go. Move forward with conﬁ dence and courage, 
ready to shape the future and make your mark in the world.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS

Thesis:
The Changing Nature of Strategic Research Management at  Selected South African 
Universities, 1997-2007

Description:
This study investigates changes in the nature of research management in three South African 
universities from 1997 to 2007. It analyses institutional change strategies and the emergence 
of  universities  as  strategic  actors  as  they  sought  to  respond  to  post-apartheid  policy, 
planning  and  funding  steering  mechanisms.  The  emergence  of  strategic  actorhood  is 
evident  in  a  shift  in  the  approach  to  research  management,  from  a  facilitatory  to  a  more 
directive  mode.  The  case  studies  demonstrate  how  the  ambiguities  around  university 
leaders’ strategic choices determine organisational action at three levels – senior leadership, 
deans, academics – across which initiatives to redress historical inequalities often compete 
with the new public management reform agenda and a marketised higher education.

Thesis:
Mediating children’s development through storytelling and play activities: a socio-cultural 
study of a Waldorf kindergarten in Cape Town 

Description:
The  study  investigated  the  role  of  storytelling  in  early  childhood  development  and  the 
connection  with  free  imaginative  play  of  children.  It  utilised  socio-cultural  theories  of  Lev 
Vygotsky as a theoretical lens, speciﬁ cally the critical role of social interaction in children’s 
learning — a continuous process that is profoundly inﬂ uenced by culture. Imitation, guided 
learning  and  collaborative  learning  feature  prominently  in  his  theory.  The  study  was 
conducted  in  a  Waldorf  kindergarten  and  centred  on  the  internalisation  of  language  in 
storytelling  and  its  expression  in  play.  The  ﬁ ndings  accentuate  the  alignment  between 
internalisation of language with imagination, zone of proximal development, private speech, 
self-regulation and identity formation.

Rethinking representation of African identity and belonging  in a selection of south

Description:
The thesis foregrounds the representation of identity politics in a selection of works by black 
South  African  writers  from  1930  to  1990,  with  a  speciﬁ c  focus  on  Herbert  Dhlomo,  Bloke 
Modisane, Wally Serote, Lauretta Ngcobo, Phaswane Mpe and Black Consciousness poets, 
Oswald  Mtshali  and  Sipho  Sepamla.  The  thesis  transcends  the  race-based  theoretical 
premise on identity and makes an alternate exploration of space as a cultural signiﬁ er in 
manifesting  identity  politics.  The  study  analysed  the  texts  through  a  decolonial  lens  with 
particular emphasis on power and resistance, and affi  rms black protest writings as sites for 
deﬁ ance against marginality, racial oppression and violation of human rights.

Thesis:
Publishing in English and its implications for researchers and higher education institutions 
in multilingual contexts in Africa: A multiple case study

Description:
The thesis examined the impact of publishing research in English at non-Anglophone African 
universities.  It  highlighted  the  complexity  of  language  on  research  quality  and  quantity, 
access to resources, the decolonisation and internationalisation of research, and the shift 
towards  research-intensive  universities.  There  is  a  marked  tension  between  English  as 
gateway to global knowledge systems and linguistic injustice. Bibliometric data was used to 
assess language and research publishing landscapes and provided robust case descriptions 
and qualitative data. Bourdieu’s notion of language as a form of cultural capital resonates 
with the perception of English as an essential asset in spite of the signiﬁ cant burden it places 
on scientists who speak a diff erent ﬁ rst language.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

HEADER

UNIVERSITY OF THE WESTERN CAPE
SUB-HEADER

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s first black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its first website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the first university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

PROF B MEZMUR

Thesis:
Legal responses to the right to nationality and prevention of statelessness among 
children in Africa

Description:
There are at least 10 million stateless people in the world. The candidate explores the legal 
responses of African countries to ensure the right to nationality and prevent statelessness 
among  children.  It  forcefully  argues  that  ensuring  the  right  to  nationality  and  preventing 
statelessness among children would be futile if it fails to take child protection systems as its 
core.  Considering  historical  and  political  debates  in  Africa,  the  thesis  identifies  common 
trends  of  statelessness  among  children  in  the  context  of  old  and  emerging  dynamics.  It 
identifies  gaps  in  protection  under  the  nationality  provisions  of  international  laws  and 
proposes mechanisms that should be adopted. The thesis presents its conclusions focusing 
on two major gaps: the general lack of a pan-African orientation on matters of nationality, 
and gaps in legislative measures including discriminatory provisions.

PROF J MUJUZI

Thesis:
Safeguarding the right to freedom from arbitrary detention in Cameroon 

Description:
Arbitrary detention is a human rights violation. International and national human rights bodies 
are doing their best to combat it. Although arbitrary detention is prohibited under international 
law  and  in  Cameroonian  law,  this  study  shows  that  it  is  widespread  and  practised 
systematically by security agencies in almost all parts of Cameroon and with impunity. The 
candidate relies on, inter alia, international law and best practices from other parts of the 
world,  to  suggest  practical  ways  in  which  the  government  of  Cameroon  can  eradicate 
arbitrary  detention.  Many  government  officials,  human  rights  activists,  students  and  legal 
practitioners in Cameroon and other parts of the world will find the recommendations in this 
study useful in their effort to fight against arbitrary detention.

Thesis:
Women’s access to land in Uganda 

Description:
The main objective of the study was to analyse policies and legal framework on women’s 
land rights in Uganda vis-à-vis Uganda’s regional and international obligations, to identify 
the progress made, gaps and make practical recommendations. To achieve this objective, 
the  candidate  analysed  the  legal  framework  on  the  women’s  land  rights  in  Uganda  and 
women’s land rights in East Africa and the nexus between women’s land rights and financial 
inclusion. The study identified several gaps in policies and legislation and recommended 
how they could be addressed. Policy makers in Uganda and other African countries will find 
the findings and recommendations of the study useful in initiating and implementing policies 
for increasing women’s access to land.

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent

award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s ﬁ rst black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its ﬁ rst website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the ﬁ rst university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Offi  ce to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff  
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest

Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and ﬁ nal Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

Thesis:
Developing Learners’ Spatial Skills and Geometric Thinking via Instructional Based 
Learning of Cyclic Quadrilateral Theorems

Description:
This  mixed  methods  study  examined  the  eff ect  of  instructional  based  learning  of  cyclic 
quadrilateral  theorems  on  grade  11  learners’  development  of  spatial  skills  and  geometric 
thinking. A conceptual framework embracing geometric thought through visualisation skills 
paved  the  way  for  Amevor  Godfred  to  use  instructional  based  learning  (IBL)  to  enable 
leaners  to  discover  and  apply  cyclic  quadrilateral  theorems  to  solve  geometric  riders. 
Findings show that IBL has a positive impact on learners’ spatial skills, active participation 
geometric reasoning, thinking and proving capabilities, and problem-solving competency.  
Integral to this study is the integration of IBL and Dynamic Geometric Environments for the 
development of learners’ spatial skills and geometric cognition.

HAMIDU IBRAHIM BUKARI

Supervisor:  

SCHOOL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS
PROF R GOVENDER

Thesis:
An investigation of the eff ect of teacher trainees’ competencies with the mathematical 
modelling processes and their reﬂ ective thinking ability on tasks

Description:
The  mixed  methods  study  investigated  the  eff ect  of  teacher  trainees’  competencies  with 
mathematical  modelling  processes  and  their  reﬂ ective  thinking  ability  on  tasks  in  the 
Ghanaian context using semi-structured interviews, a questionnaire, and a test.  A purposeful 
homogenous sampling technique was used to obtain a sample of 231 teacher trainees for 
the survey, with 35 in the comparison group and 38 in the treatment group. A propensity 
score analysis of graphs was employed to conﬁ rm the conceptual model’s applicability and

Investigating the English Language Proﬁ ciency and Communication Skills of First-Year

Description:
The study examines English proﬁ ciency and communication skills of ﬁ rst-year students at 
the  University  of  Namibia  Khomasdal  Campus.  Based  on  Interactionist  and  Constructivist 
theories, it takes a qualitative approach to prospect and analyse causes and eff ects of any 
discrepancy.  The  study  stems  from  lecturers’  sentiment  that  students  lack  suffi  cient 
communication skills. This deﬁ ciency is attributed to poor proﬁ ciency although English has 
always been the primary LoLT in Namibia. The Namibian language policy and the inﬂ uence 
of vernacular languages also contribute to poor English proﬁ ciency. Major impediments to 
eff ective  communication  include  among  others  oral  language  inadequacy  and  limited 
speaking activities. The study suggests an entrance course prioritising the students’ needs.

The thesis exempliﬁ es the pedagogical serviceability of literature texts in the English Access 
Course off ered to high school leaving learners entering the University of Namibia. The study 
investigates how the use of peer assessment and role play as response in the reading of 
literature can help students become motivated readers. The study argues that the accruing 
reading  ability  can  optimize  their  conﬁ dence  and  motivations  for  tackling  more  complex

conﬁ rmatory support point to some factors that can impede their reading of literature, while 
attesting to the potential that literature texts have for sublimating their higher order thinking 
skills via peer assessment and role play. The study affi  rms that these skills can shield them 
from the perils of skim reading in an age synonymous with a rampant inability to read the

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Dear Graduands,

Welcome to UWC’s first graduation ceremonies of 2023. Congratulations to you 
and to all who supported you, your parents, guardians, loved ones and friends.

Today  you  will  experience  what  it  means  to  achieve  success  through  hard 
work and determination. As you settle into your seat in the Jakes Gerwel Hall, 
take a moment to reflect on what this journey has meant to you. Think about 
the many hours you had to invest in your studies. As with any good investment, 
you  are  now  reaping  the  rewards  of  the  sacrifices  you  have  made  and  the 
challenges you have overcome.

As you cast your mind’s eye over your student experience here at the University 
of the Western Cape, remember your very first day on campus, your first lecture 
and tutorial. I’m sure you can recall the nervous anxiety you felt on that first day. 

Now, at last, you have completed the journey of being a student. But many 
other new journeys await you. They will test your strength of character 
and,  perhaps,  your  integrity  and  sense  of  purpose.  They  will 

also demand your time and dedication. 

But  take  the  lessons  you  have  learned  at  UWC  with 
you: remember the times when the road became almost 
too  long,  and  it  felt  as  if  you  were  ready  to  give  up.  You 
didn’t! You persevered and succeeded. You acquired vital skills 
such as patience, resilience and perseverance. These will stand 
you in good stead wherever you go in the years ahead.

Again, my heartfelt congratulations on your achievements and 

best wishes for your future endeavours.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA
UWC CHANCELLOR

MESSAGE FROM THE RECTOR
HEADER

SUB-HEADER

Every time we celebrate important milestones at the University of the Western 
Cape, I do so with a deep sense of appreciation because, not so long ago, we 
didn’t know when we would have the opportunity to gather together again.

This  graduation  ceremony  therefore  serves  as  a  reminder  of  how  uncertain 
our lives were and how fundamentally it had changed.

Even now, with the imminent threat of the COVID-19 pandemic behind us, the 
uncertainty of that time seems to linger.

It makes it then even more important to use moments such as these to reflect 
on how we did not allow defeatism to set in, but rather how we determined our 
way to get to this point.

You,  our  students,  are  gaining  your  diplomas  and  degrees  are  proof  of  that 
determination. Through your resilience and ability, you adapted to circumstances 
that were unfamiliar to you. Many of you might have wondered how you would 
get to this point while being deprived of the comfort and familiarity of 
campus, lectures and your classmates.

But  here  you  are  and  we  salute  you.  We  also  thank  your 
parents, guardian and loved ones for supporting you throughout 
your academic careers and walking this challenging journey with you.

We are proud of you, our newest graduates and know that you will 
go out into the world with pride and determination, ready to take on 
the next chapter of your lives.

PROF. TYRONE PRETORIUS 
RECTOR AND VICE-CHANCELLOR

1960:  The University College of the 
Western Cape opens its doors.

1970:   The institution gains independent 
university status and is allowed to 
award its own degrees and diplomas.

1975:   Prof Richard van der Ross is 

appointed as UWC’s first black Rector.

1978:   UWC’s Cape Flats Nature Reserve is 
declared a National Monument (now 
known as a provincial heritage site).

1987:   New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Prof 

Jakes Gerwel, declares UWC as the 
‘university of the left’. The University 
deracialises and opens its doors to 
African students.

1995:  UWC launches its first website 

– joining the internet age before other 
universities in the Mother City.

UWC launches the Institute for 
Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies 
(PLAAS) to engage in research, 
training, policy development and 
advocacy in relation to land reform, 
rural governance and natural 
resource management.

2002:  Under the leadership of Rector and 

Vice-Chancellor, Prof Brian O’Connell, 
UWC successfully resists being 
merged. Instead, its Dentistry Faculty 
is merged with that of the University of 
Stellenbosch, making UWC the only 
dentistry faculty in the Western Cape.

UWC inaugurates its longest-serving 
Chancellor, Archbishop Desmond 
Tutu, who would serve for more than 
25 years.

2010:   10 SARChI chairs awarded to UWC, 
the highest number awarded to any 
university in SA that year (as of 2018, 
UWC hosts 17 SARChI Chairs).

1990:   UWC becomes the first university to 
award the late President Mandela an 
honorary doctorate upon his release 
from prison.

1994:   Many academics from UWC join 

President Mandela’s government and 
are appointed to ministerial and 
advisory positions, including its Rector, 
Prof Gerwel, who became the 
Director-General in the Presidency.

2012:   UWC launches its Technology 

Transfer Office to help promote the 
development and protection of the 
intellectual property of the 
University’s research community, staff 
and students.

UWC is declared Africa’s Greenest 
Campus in the inaugural African 
Green Campus Initiative Challenge.

UWC’s leadership takes part in 
writing the higher education policy 
for the incoming government. The 
South African interim Constitution 
and final Constitution are drafted 
at UWC.

2013:   UWC signs the Berlin Declaration on 

Open Access in the Sciences and 
Humanities, joining hundreds of 
institutions around the world dedicated 
to supporting the principles of open 
access and working to achieve 
openness in publicly funded projects.

PUBLIC LAW AND JURISPRUDENCE
PROF E DUROJAYE

Thesis:
Indigenous women’s access to sexual and reproductive health rights in Zimbabwe: A 
case of the San community in Tsholotsho and Plumtree

Description:
The  thesis  addresses  an  important  aspect  of  reproductive  health  and  rights  of  indigenous 
women  in  Zimbabwe.  It  specifically  focuses  on  the  barriers  that  indigenous  women  face  in 
accessing reproductive health services. Anchoring the analysis in a rights-based approach, and 
within  the  theoretical  frameworks  of  intersectionality  and  substantive  equality,  the  study 
examines  the  norms  and  standards  existing  at  the  international  and  regional  levels  for  the 
realisation  of  the  right  to  reproductive  health  for  indigenous  women.  All  the  examiners  are 
unanimous  in  affirming  the  significant  contribution  of  this  study,  including  providing  “cutting-
edge insight” into the field of reproductive health, not only in Zimbabwe but in Africa as a whole.

SIPHO NKOSI

Department:  
Supervisor:  
Co-supervisor:   PROF Y MUPANGAVANHU

PRIVATE LAW
PROF L MWAMBENE

Thesis:
Ubuntu and the South African Law of Contract With Particular Reference to the Common 
Law Contract of Employment 

Description:
The debate on the role that ubuntu can assist in bringing about greater social justice and fairness 
in many areas, including education, criminal law, property law, contract law, and employment law, 
is ongoing. Mr Nkosi, through his thesis demonstrates how ubuntu can be used, and is being 
used already, to create new rights and procedures, resuscitate some of the old common law 
remedies, develop and enhance existing ones, or to discard the old ones that do not resonate 
with  the  letter  and  spirit  of  the  Constitution.  Mr  Nkosi’s  thesis,  therefore,  makes  a  significant 
contribution in its quest for a more equitable legal regime of contract law, and the common law 
contract  of  employment.  Moreover,  and  as  correctly  observed  by  two  of  his  examiners,  Mr 
Nkosi’s thesis, demonstrate how the South African law of contract in general is in need of the 
kind of redemptive transformation that only ubuntu could help bring about social justice.

Supervisor:  
Co-supervisor:   DR A RAMANANTOANINA

MATHEMATICS
PROF K PATIDAR

Thesis:
Analysis and robust simulation of mathematical models of HIV and Leishmaniasis 
co-infection

Description:
Visceral Leishmaniasis (VL) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) are mutually reinforcing, 
posing clinical and public health issues. In endemic areas, HIV infections increase the risk of 
developing  VL  by  100  to  2320  times,  reduce  the  likelihood  of  therapeutic  response,  and 
immensely increase the probability of relapse. The co-infection of VL and HIV is reported from 
forty-five countries since the first case was reported in 1985. Through mathematical modelling, 
Elias  in  this  work  did  theoretical  and  numerical  studies  of  these  co-infection  models.  He 
presented  an  elegant  mathematical  analysis  through  the  geometric  singular  perturbation 
theory  and  then  developed  dynamically  consistent  numerical  methods  to  obtain  reliable 
simulation results.

GETACHEW TILAHUN AFFESA

Department:  
Supervisor:  
Co-supervisor:   DR A RAMANANTOANINA

MATHEMATICS
PROF K PATIDAR

Thesis:
Analysis and simulation of mathematical models governing HIV-TB co-infection dynamics 
in Ethiopia

Description:
Despite several advancements in the medical sciences and health care systems, the impact of 
HIV-TB co-infection remains the most prominent health challenge of the 21st century. In addition 
to being one of the main factors that contribute to morbidity and mortality, HIV and TB also have 
a detrimental impact that adds to the burden on the healthcare system. In his thesis, Getachew 
analysed systems of nonlinear differential equations describing the co-infection of these two 
diseases.  He  used  a  geometric  singular  perturbation  theory,  which  is  a  very  complicated 
approach, to study the slow-fast dynamics described through these models. He then developed 
a range of non-standard finite difference schemes to efficiently simulate these models. 

13

2023FACULTY OF NATURAL SCIENCESDOCTOR’S DEGREESDOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHYGRADUATION CEREMONY 2023YESHAMBEL AZENE BELAY

Department:  
Supervisor:  
Co-supervisor:   DR A RAMANANTOANINA

MATHEMATICS
PROF K PATIDAR

Thesis:
Analysis and simulation of some ecological models describing weed-water hyacinth 
dynamics in Lake Tana, Ethiopia

Description:
The water hyacinth plant is notorious for being the world’s worst aquatic weed. Yeshambel 
considered systems of nonlinear differential equations modelling the water hyacinth effect 
in  lake  ecosystems.  These  models  include  the  refuge  effect  of  water  hyacinths  in  lake 
ecosystems, the effect of water hyacinths in the lake eutrophication dynamics and singularly 
perturbed (slow-fast) phytoplankton-zooplankton systems, and predator-prey systems with 
water hyacinth’s refuge effect. The slow-fast systems are characterized by the presence of 
a very small positive parameter representing the separation of time-scales between the fast 
and slow dynamics. Yeshambel presented a rigorous qualitative and quantitative analysis of 
such models and has drawn meaningful conclusions from his studies.

THOMAS JOEL FARRAR 

Department:  
Supervisor:  
Co-supervisors:   DR R LUUS,  PROF S STEEL

STATISTICS AND POPULATION STUDIES
PROF R BLIGNAUT

Thesis:
Handling heteroscedasticity in the linear regression model

Description:
Thomas’s  thesis  investigated  the  problem  of  violation  of  the  assumption  of  variance 
homogeneity  in  the  linear  regression  model,  a  very  widely  used  statistical  method.  This 
phenomenon is often observed in cross-sectional data and adversely affects both estimation 
and inference. To address this problem, new statistical theory was developed in the form of 
a  class  of  models  called  Auxiliary  Variance  Models.  The  models  were  refined  and  then 
evaluated  empirically  using  Monte  Carlo  simulation  experiments.  They  were  found  to 
outperform  existing  methods  under  some  conditions.  To  make  the  new  methods  readily 
accessible to statistics practitioners, functions were written in the R programming language 
and published as a package called skedastic in R statistical software.

CHEMISTRY
PROF E IWUOHA

Thesis:
Interferon-gamma aptasensor for ultrasensitive TB diagnostics

Description:
The World Health Organisation estimated the occurrence of 10 million TB illnesses in 2020, 
of which only 5.8 million received diagnostic tests and treatment, and thus proposed point-
of-care  biomarker  diagnostics  as  a  way  improving  the  test-treatment  levels.  Interferon 
gamma is recognised as a very important TB disease biomarker which is suitable for early 
screening. The TB aptasensor invention of Kaylin Januarie, is a biochemically customised 
DNA sensor chip that has high affinity for interferon gamma, which is coupled to the ultra-
sensitive  electrochemical  signalling  of  novel  telluride-selenide  dichalcogenide  quantum 
dot. The study involved a cooperation with the Interfibio Research Group in the Department 
of Chemical Engineering, University of Rovira I Virgili, Spain. 

ERIKA KAPP

SCHOOL OF PHARMACY
Supervisor:  
PROF S MALAN
Co-supervisors:   PROF J JOUBERT,  PROF S SAMPSON

Thesis:
Evaluation of selected polycyclic compounds as resistance modulators in 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Description:
Antimicrobial resistance in M tuberculosis (Mtb) is of particular concern as South Africa falls in 
the  top  7  countries  with  the  highest  MDR  TB  incidence.  In  this  study,  Erika  explored  the 
possibility of addressing drug resistance in Mtb through the evaluation of polycyclic compounds 
for antimycobacterial activity and synergism with known drugs through efflux pump inhibition. 
To this end, a homology model of the Rv1258c efflux pump was developed to visualize protein-
ligand interactions and to facilitate identification and design of novel structures. Polycyclic and 
coumarin derivatives with low micromolar antimycobacterial activity were identified. The most 
promising  compound,  an  adamantane  amide  derivative  was  found  to  affect  MmpL3,  a 
mycobacterial  membrane  protein  essential  for  bacterial  survival.  Selected  polycyclic 
compounds showed synergism ascribed to inhibition of Rv1258c.

Thesis:
Electrochemical signalling and wireless oxidative incineration of environmental 
antiretrovirals with bipolar boron-doped diamond microdots reactor 

Description:
The preponderance of HIV in South Africa (7.5 million cases in 2021 of which 5.5 million of them 
were  on  antiretroviral  treatment),  necessitates  the  inclusion  of  antiretroviral  drugs  and  their 
metabolites in the water contaminants inventory.  Kefilwe Vanessa Mokwebo developed a next 
generation electrochemical reactor for the sensing and annihilation of antiretrovirals pollutants in 
water. Her invention consists of concentrated high electric-field bipolar boron-doped diamond 
microparticulate electrodes with no wire connections. The wireless microparticulate electrodes 
provided  large  surface  area  and  wide  potential  window  for  the  electrooxidation  of  organic 
chemicals. Part of this work was done at the National University of Ireland, Maynooth, and in 
collaboration with the National Centre for Sensor Research at Dublin City University Ireland.

Thesis:
Electro-photovoltaics of palladium kesterites functionalised with terbium and europium 
doped yttrium and gadolinium oxyselenides 

Description:
The prevailing quest for non-fossil fuel energy due to climate change realities, has led to 
intensive research for novel, affordable and sustainable solar cell materials. Kesterite are 
naturally  occurring  minerals  with  excellent  propensity  as  replacements  for  expensive 
crystalline silicon that is currently used in commercial solar panels. Kelechi Nwambaekwe 
engineered the light absorption properties of kesterites to produce solar cell devices with 
enhanced photovoltaic performance. This he achieved by incorporating small amounts of 
photoelectroactive compounds containing specific rare-earth metals (europium, gadolinium, 
terbium and yttrium) into palladium kesterite nanomaterial. Aspects of this work were done 
at the Institute of Applied Physics of the Academy of Sciences of Moldova.

MEANING AND SYMBOLISM

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded effect is meant to reflect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHANCELLOR

HEADER

SUB-HEADER

We warmly welcome you as we celebrate the culmination of your remarkable 
journey at the University of the Western Cape. Today represents the beginning 
of a new and exciting chapter for each of our graduating students. To the parents, 
guardians, families, and educators who supported you, your encouragement and 
sacriﬁ ces have played a big role in the success of our graduands. We applaud 
your collective contributions.

As you, the graduands, reﬂ ect on your journey to this day, remember the initial 
excitement, and the anxiety. From the moment of your very ﬁ rst lecture, to the 
dedication shown through countless late nights of studying. Think about how 
you forged lifelong friendships on campus. Acknowledge the challenges you 
overcame, the doubts you conquered, and the resilience that has shaped you 
into the person you are today. Look around you at your fellow graduands, the 
friends  with  whom  you  shared  laughter,  tears,  and  an  incredible  academic 
journey. Recognise the common ground you built during your time at UWC - the 
unspoken bonds forged through shared experiences, and how you transformed 
into scholars, leaders, and changemakers. Your journey at UWC has been 
extraordinary, marked by global and local challenges. This makes your 
resilience  and  dedication,  and  unﬂ inching  spirit  even  more 
remarkable. Facing disruptions, uncertainties, and new ways 
of learning, you contributed actively to our community by 
demonstrating perseverance and commitment to growth. 
This is a testament to your strength and character. 

Never forget the transformative power of education, the community 
that supported your dreams, and the values that shaped your path. 
As you embark on your new journey, know that the UWC family 
stands behind you, forever connected by the shared experiences 
of  your  time  here.  A  ﬁ nal  word:  please  make  sure  you  are 
registered to vote in this year’s national and provincial elections. 
Study the manifestos of the various parties, evaluate the 
quality of their leaders, and use your vote wisely. The 

future of South Africa depends on it. 

Congratulations, Class of 2024. The world awaits 
you, and I have no doubt that you will rise to 
the challenge.

THE MOST REVEREND DR THABO CECIL MAKGOBA

As we celebrate this signiﬁ cant occasion in the life of the University of the 
Western Cape, I am ﬁ lled with an overwhelming sense of pride and gratitude 
for what you, our graduating class of 2024 has accomplished. This graduation 
ceremony  is  a  special  moment  that  serves  as  a  poignant  reminder  of  our 
collective resilience and enduring spirit.

But it is not only a celebration of academic achievements, it is also a testament 
to your determination, adaptability, and perseverance. Against the backdrop of 
ongoing  global  challenges,  you  have  each  forged  your  path  to  success, 
embodying the true essence of what it means to be a student at UWC.
Your journey to this day has undoubtedly been marked by obstacles, yet your 
resolve  to  overcome  them  has  been  inspirational.  Whether  navigating  the 
complexities  of  remote  learning,  and  the  absence  of  traditional  campus  life, 
you have demonstrated exceptional strength and character.

Today, it is essential to acknowledge not only your hard-earned achievements 
but also the support of your parents, guardians, families, and loved ones. Their 
encouragement and belief in your potential have been pivotal to your 
journey. And for that, we extend our deepest gratitude. As 
you begin the next phase of your journey, know that you do 
so with our full support and admiration. 

Always remember, you are equipped with the knowledge, skills, 
and values you need to make a diff erence, no matter where life 
takes you. Take pride in how far you have come, and have faith in 
how far you can go. Move forward with conﬁ dence and courage, 
ready to shape the future and make your mark in the world.

Thesis:
Assessing the adequacy of government trusteeship as a tool for attaining sustainable 
development in community land management: a case study of Turkana county, Kenya

Description:
The thesis explores land management of unregistered community land under county government 
trusteeship  against  the  backdrop  of  legal  norms  that  require  equitable,  sustainable  and 
productive management of land. The case study of Turkana County (Kenya) shows that land 
management is in fact characterised by illegal land dispositions, lack of access to land, crippled 
economic growth, and non-participatory community land governance. With reference to land 
management practices in South Africa and Mozambique as well as theories on state trusteeship, 
the study identiﬁ es distinct elements that hinder eff ective land management, in light of which it 
urges for the reform of community land laws in Kenya. The study makes a valuable contribution 
to policy discussions on land reform for the sustainable use of rural Africa.

proposes necessary improvements to enhance the Critical Skills Work Visa programme. The 
thesis,  based  on  a  comprehensive  comparative  analysis,  recommends  measures  to  align 
South Africa’s immigration framework with international benchmarks, address inconsistencies 
in application, and establish a proactive immigration regime that can eff ectively address skill 
shortages and promote economic growth.

Thesis:
Corporate Social Responsibility Provisions in African Regional Trade and Investment 
Agreements: Critical Legal Analysis and Construction of an Alternative Approach for the 
African Market

Description:
The thesis investigates the regulatory framework for Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) in 
African  Regional  Trade  and  Investment  Agreements  (RTIAs).  It  proposes  an  alternative 
approach to enhance CSR eff ectiveness in Africa, aimed at boosting corporations’ contributions 
to inclusive and sustainable development. The study analyses 13 RTIAs from 2000 - 2020 in 
West African and Southern African regions. Employing legal and document analysis methods, 
the research identiﬁ es a unique regulatory approach in African RTIAs, combining mandatory 
and voluntary elements, but lacking a strong foundation in Ubuntu. The proposed solution, 
termed the ‘Africanised Approach to CSR regulation’, integrates Ubuntu, to strengthen CSR 
provisions, aimed towards inclusive and sustainable development in Africa.

Description:
The  thesis  addresses  a  very  important  issue  in  relation  to  the  right  to  food  in  Uganda.  It 
argues that despite the fact that Uganda has made commitments under international and 
regional human rights instruments to realise the right to food, this right remains unrealisable 
for millions of people in the country. Using the legal empowerment concept, the thesis notes 
that if the people are well empowered to understand the nature of the right to food, they are 
likely to hold the government accountable and ensure eff ective realisation of this right at the 
national level. This thesis has made important contribution to the realisation of the right to 
food in Uganda.

Thesis:
Implementing the Spatial and Land Use Management Act of 2013: an examination of the 
intersection of the role of traditional leaders and municipalities in spatial planning and 
land use management 

Description:
The candidate examines the intersection of the role of traditional leaders in land allocation, 
and the role of municipalities in spatial planning and land use management. He traces the 
history  of  land  tenure  in  communal  areas  back  to  pre-colonial  times  and  discusses  the 
chequered history of traditional leadership during colonialism and apartheid. The candidate 
then discusses the emergence of democratic local government in 2000, and the introduction 
of ‘wall-to-wall’ municipal town planning in terms of the new Spatial Planning and Land Use 
Management Act. On the basis of interviews with traditional leaders and other stakeholders, 
he presents a comprehensive analysis of the deep conﬂ ict between traditional leaders and 
municipalities about who controls the use of communal land. Using a theoretical framework 
of  legal  integration,  as  well  as  a  pragmatic  approach  to  conﬂ ict  resolution,  he  presents 
recommendations on how the conﬂ ict can be resolved.

The three proteas symbolise Teaching, Culture 
and Education.

The stepped pattern represents the steps that lead to 
the Greek temple. This is the international symbol for 
academia and our recognition that we are a part of it.

The laurel leaves indicate competition 
and victory.

The diamond-shaped protea petal represents 
strength of character, ethics and faithfulness to 
oneself and others.

The continuous pattern that extends from the front 
to the back speaks to Respice Prospice, which 
means to look back, to look forward. Take what is 
good from the past and build the future.

The beaded eff ect is meant to reﬂ ect African craft 
and creativity.

The colours that make up the band are derived 
from those that represent the seven Faculties that 
make up the University.

CORE ACTIVITIES OF

CASAS 

•  Harmonisation and standardisation of cluster 

language orthographies; 

•  Promotion of local languages in basic education; 

•  Production and dissemination of literacy textbooks, 
textbooks for citizenship education, vocational and 
out-of-school training; 

•  Research on African linguistics and language 

policies; 

•  Organisation of workshops, conferences, seminars 
and colloquia on various topics as approved by its 
Scientific Advisory Board (SAB). 

Publication types from the CASAS Network

•  Book Series with titles on aspects of linguistics 

and sociolinguistics written by individual authors 
or as editions of papers presented at conferences, 
workshops and seminars; 

•  Monographs which include the orthographies and 
informative texts on matters of concern to the 
general public such as health, agriculture and social 
issues as well as on education and linguistics; 

•  Notes and Records which predominantly cover 

areas of linguistics; 

•  Occasional Papers (following on from the Notes and 

Records) 

•  Tinabantu – a journal with articles on African issues 

other than linguistics; 

•  Primers and Readers for use in schools 

•  Glossaries 

•  Monolingual Dictionaries
